chunk_findings.detail: The fixture creates a real git commit without pinning the commit dates (`GIT_AUTHOR_DATE` / `GIT_COMMITTER_DATE` are absent from the environment fixture, which only scrubs `DDFLOW_*`, `FORCE_COLOR`, `NO_COLOR` and sets `COLUMNS`). `git commit` fills author/committer date with the current wall-clock (and the local timezone offset), and both are part of the object that is hashed. So the SHA of `HEAD` — and therefore of every derived short/long hash — is different on every run and on every machine. The fixture exists precisely because ddflow surfaces git provenance (the whole point of `git init`/`config`/`commit` here is to give the brief/recall/exports a stable repo), so any golden that prints the HEAD sha (e.g. the brief header, or an export that records `git rev-parse HEAD`) is non-deterministic: run `uv run pytest tests/golden` twice, or run it on a machine in a different timezone, and the snapshot diffs even though no code changed. The fix is to export fixed `GIT_AUTHOR_DATE`/`GIT_COMMITTER_DATE` (and clear any inherited `GIT_*`) around the commit.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/conftest.py `project` fixture (the `git commit -qm "init"` call)

chunk_findings.detail: `re.sub(rf"(?<![\w.]){re.escape(__version__)}(?![\w.])", ...)` will not replace the version whenever the character immediately before it is a word character. Given the common CLI spelling `ddflow v0.1.0`, the preceding char is `v` (a `\w`), so the negative lookbehind fails, no substitution happens, and the raw version string is baked into the golden. The same is true for a build-string form such as `0.1.0.dev0`, where the trailing `.` in the lookahead `(?![\w.])` also blocks the match. In those cases the normaliser silently does nothing and the golden breaks on the next version bump — the exact failure it is supposed to prevent — rather than being version-independent. (Conditional on the CLI printing the version adjacent to a word char/dot; a plain `ddflow 0.1.0` does match.)
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/conftest.py `normalise` version regex

chunk_findings.detail: The `id` on the `research.recorded` line is `e74721cbed98fa006bd15157d`, which is 25 hex characters, while every other id in this fixture (and the writer's generated ids, which are 24-hex) is exactly 24. The whole point of the fixture is to exercise real writer payload shapes, so this is an invalid shape. Concretely: if the event loader validates id width/format when reading the JSONL, loading this fixture raises and every golden/property test built on it fails with a load error rather than exercising behaviour; if the loader happens not to validate, the property tests then pin behaviour for an id no real writer can emit, i.e. the "properties hold for real writer payload shapes" guarantee is lost for this record. Either way the snapshot/golden suite is testing an unreachable input. Fixing it to a 24-hex id (and regenerating any snapshot whose subject/subject-derived value comes from this id, e.g. `R49b608db82`) is needed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/fixtures/project.jsonl:9 (event `R49b608db82` / `research.recorded`)

chunk_findings.detail: `unwrap_usage` normalises only the first paragraph (`text.partition("\n\n")`). But argparse computes its layout width from the *environment*, not from the snapshot: `HelpFormatter.__init__` does `width = shutil.get_terminal_size().columns - 2`, and `shutil.get_terminal_size()` returns `int(os.environ["COLUMNS"])` when that variable is set, otherwise the size of `sys.__stdout__.fileno()` (which succeeds when capture is disabled, e.g. `pytest -s` on a real terminal) and only falls back to 80 when both are unavailable. The description and the `options:`/`positional arguments:` sections are filled/wrapped at that width (`_fill_text`, `_format_action`), and none of that is normalised by `unwrap_usage`, which only touches the `usage` paragraph. Concrete repro: `COLUMNS=40 pytest tests/golden/test_golden_cli_help.py::test_help` (or running the file with `-s` in a terminal wider/narrower than 80 columns) produces `format_help()` whose description/option help wraps at different points than the .ambr recorded at width 78, so the assertion fails although the CLI interface is unchanged. This contradicts the stated goal that the goldens be deterministic across machines. Passing an explicit width to the parser/formatter (or whitespace-normalising every paragraph, not just the first) is needed to make this golden environment-independent.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/test_golden_cli_help.py:52 (`unwrap_usage` / `test_help`)

chunk_findings.detail: The guard filters candidate document names with `r.islower() and r.isalpha()`, so its set of "documents" is restricted to strings in `[a-z]+`. That defeats the stated purpose ("A new export document must be added to EXPORTS, or it ships unpinned") for any name that is not pure lowercase ASCII letters: a name containing a digit, hyphen, or underscore is dropped from `rows` by the filter before comparison. Concretely, if the CLI later adds an export document `release-notes` (or `v2worklog`), and the maintainer correctly adds `"release-notes"` to `EXPORTS`, `rows` never contains it, so `rows == EXPORTS` fails even though the listing is correct — a false failure. In the other direction, if the maintainer forgets to add `release-notes` to `EXPORTS`, the filter also drops it from `rows`, so the check passes vacuously and the new document ships unpinned. The same filter also silently discards any unindented lowercase-alpha footer/usage token (e.g. a line beginning `run ...`), which would turn into a spurious row and a false failure if such a line is ever emitted. The check should compare the listing's document column structurally rather than by an ad-hoc alphabetic heuristic.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/test_golden_outputs.py:35 (`test_the_export_list_names_every_document_pinned_here`)

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring of `event_logs` states the returned list is "A merged log in the order `read_all` returns it: ... sorted by (lamport, agent, id) **and de-duplicated**", but the body only does `return sorted(out, key=Event.sort_key)` — no de-duplication step exists. Because the whole premise of the generator (spelled out in the same docstring) is that "clones that did not see each other can reuse a value", two independently generated events can coincide on the fields that determine an event's identity (`kind`, `subject`, `data`, and the reused Lamport value), i.e. they are the same event id; `read_all` collapses such a pair to a single event, whereas this strategy emits both. Any property that is supposed to pin read_all semantics (e.g. "replay equals live", or a fold whose result depends on the number/ordering of events) is therefore exercised on a log that `read_all` can never return, so it can fail — or pass vacuously because the duplicate is folded as if it were two distinct events — for reasons that do not exist in production. The fix is to merge on the event id (e.g. keep the first/last per id before/after sorting) so the fixture actually matches the documented `read_all` output.
chunk_findings.title: tests/property/evstrategies.py:146 (`event_logs`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The assertion compares a deduplicated input on the left with the raw generated log on the right:

```python
assert _sorted_unique(shuffled) == _sorted_unique(events)          # ok
assert fold(_sorted_unique(shuffled), strict=False) == fold(events, strict=False)
```

The left operand is the normalized union (`_sorted_unique` collapses repeated events); the right operand is the un-normalized `events`. The module's stated property is only that "however the shards are concatenated, the *sorted union* folds the same" (and the sibling test `test_a_duplicated_history_folds_like_the_history_once` deliberately deduplicates **both** sides with `_sorted_unique` before folding, i.e. it treats a repeated event as fold-visible and therefore not safe to fold twice). So if the generated log ever contains the same event twice (which is exactly the situation the duplication test constructs), the two sides fold different histories: the left applies that event once, the right applies it twice, the resulting `State`s differ, and the assertion fails even though the fold is order-free as documented. The right-hand side should be `fold(_sorted_unique(events), strict=False)`; as written it pins an undocumented "fold also normalizes duplicates" property that the rest of the file does not assume.
chunk_findings.title: tests/property/test_fold_properties.py:70 (`test_the_order_shards_are_read_in_does_not_matter`)

chunk_findings.detail: The property is stated as "no two ready items' globs overlap (a shared glob overlaps nothing)", but both assertions (`not conflicts(a.globs, b.globs, shared)` and `not conflicts(it.globs, lease.globs, shared)`) call the *same* `conflicts` predicate that `schedule.plan` uses internally to decide what is offerable. This makes the check tautological with respect to `conflicts` itself: it can only detect plan failing to call `conflicts`, never a bug inside `conflicts`. Concrete vacuous pass: if a refactor makes `conflicts` return `False` for two identical non-shared globs (e.g. `conflicts(["src/a.py"], ["src/a.py"], []) == False`, e.g. by an over-eager "a shared glob overlaps nothing" carve‑out or an equality/short-circuit change), then plan will emit two ready items that genuinely both write `src/a.py`, and the assertion still passes because `conflicts` also says they don't conflict. The deps property avoids exactly this by writing its own `_deps_met`; this property does not, so the class of regression it exists to pin ("no conflicting offers") can slip through.
chunk_findings.title: tests/property/test_scheduler_properties.py:97 (`test_no_two_offers_conflict_and_none_overlaps_another_agents_lease`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The second half of the same test takes "another agent's live lease" from `state.active_leases`, which is the production helper `plan` itself relies on for lease awareness. If `active_leases` regresses (e.g. stops returning a lease whose `taken`/`heartbeat` is within `grace_s`, or mis-handles the `shared_globs` argument), the test will simply not see the lease and will pass while plan hands out an offer that collides with a live lease. A hand-rolled oracle (e.g. scanning raw lease events against `now - grace_s`) would be needed to make this check able to fail.

---

Everything else in the file (offset lamports on the tail, `fold(..., strict=False)`, `max_examples=150`/`database=None`, the free-slot bound, the bucket-partition and determinism assertions) I could not break with the generated shapes.
chunk_findings.title: tests/property/test_scheduler_properties.py:103 (lease-liveness oracle)

chunk_findings.detail: The fixture's whole stated purpose is "Nothing from the developer's shell reaches the output: no `DDFLOW_*` override (each would show as an `[env]` source)", and the loop clears every `DDFLOW_*` variable — except `DDFLOW_LAUNCH_ROOT`, which is explicitly exempted and neither cleared nor re-pinned to the temporary repo. That leaves the golden output dependent on the ambient shell, in two concrete ways. (a) If `main` reports its configuration sources (the `[env]` lines the comment is worried about), a developer who has the ddflow shell integration active, e.g. `export DDFLOW_LAUNCH_ROOT=/home/dev/realproj`, gets an extra/changed `[env] DDFLOW_LAUNCH_ROOT=...` line in `tools/list`/`brief`/`recall` output that was not present when the snapshot was recorded (CI usually has the variable unset), so the "byte-identical across machines" property fails without any code change. (b) If the CLI uses `DDFLOW_LAUNCH_ROOT` for repo/launch-root resolution, then `main(["--repo", str(project), "--agent", "golden", *argv])` is run with a value pointing at the developer's real repository rather than `tmp_path/proj`, so the captured output is produced from the wrong project — and any mutating golden test would write into that real repo instead of the fixture. Demonstration: `DDFLOW_LAUNCH_ROOT=$HOME/myproject uv run pytest tests/golden` versus a clean `env -u DDFLOW_LAUNCH_ROOT uv run pytest tests/golden`; the two runs must not be able to differ, but with the exemption in place they can. Either delete it like every other `DDFLOW_*` key, or set it explicitly to `str(project)` so it is a pinned input rather than an inherited one.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/conftest.py:33-36 (`_pinned_environment` / `DDFLOW_LAUNCH_ROOT`)

chunk_findings.detail: `format_help()` is produced by `argparse.HelpFormatter`, and when `build_parser()` does not pass an explicit `width`, the formatter derives its width from `shutil.get_terminal_size()` (i.e. the `COLUMNS` env var, else the size of fd 1, else the 80x24 fallback). `unwrap_usage` only normalises the leading `usage:` paragraph; everything after the first `\n\n` (the description and the options/arguments sections) is snapshotted raw, and those sections wrap at `self._width` (`_format_text` uses `text_width = self._width - indent`, `_format_action` derives `help_position`/`help_width` from `self._width`). So the snapshot only matches when the effective width happens to be the one used to record the `.ambr`. Concrete failure: under pytest's default fd capture the fallback is 80, but `COLUMNS=140 pytest tests/golden/test_golden_cli_help.py` (or `pytest -s` / `--capture=no` run from a 140-column terminal, which is the common way to debug) makes fd 1 a tty of width 140, `format_help()` wraps any long description or long option help at 138 columns instead of 78, and the assert fails although nothing in `ddflow/` changed. This contradicts the stated goal that the goldens are deterministic across machines; the recording and the assertion environments differ in a variable the test never pins.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/test_golden_cli_help.py: unwrap_usage / test_help

chunk_findings.detail: The guard is claimed by its own docstring to fail "or it ships unpinned" whenever a new export document appears, but the filter `[r for r in rows if r.islower() and r.isalpha()]` silently discards any row whose name is not purely lowercase alphabetic. `"release-notes".islower()` is True but `"release-notes".isalpha()` is False; `"audit2".isalpha()` is False; and any name containing `_`, `.`, or a digit is dropped the same way. So if a future export is registered as `release-notes` (or `by-file`, `audit2`, ...), the listing gains that row, the filter removes it, and the assertion still compares `[...] == EXPORTS` and passes — exactly the "ships unpinned" case the test exists to prevent. The test only catches new exports whose names happen to be pure lowercase ASCII letters. A stronger form would compare the parsed row names without the `islower`/`isalpha` narrowing (or assert that every parsed name is in `EXPORTS` and that the sets are equal) so non-alphabetic names cannot slip through.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/test_golden_outputs.py:38-41 (`test_the_export_list_names_every_document_pinned_here`)

chunk_findings.detail: `event_logs` documents itself as returning "A merged log in the order `read_all` returns it: ... sorted by (lamport, agent, id) and de-duplicated," but the function only sorts — it never de-duplicates, and it is *constructed* so that de-duplication can never matter: within one agent, `clocks[agent] = floor + draw(st.integers(1, 3))` is strictly increasing across every draw, so no two events can share `(agent, lamport)`, and each `(kind, subject, data)` is drawn exactly once. Therefore no two generated events can share an `id` (any `compute_id` that includes the agent and/or the lamport, as it must for `read_all` to be able to dedup a merged log at all, already makes them distinct here). Consequently the claimed "de-duplicated" property is never exercised: a property test of the form "fold(merged log) == fold(deduped merged log)" or "re-ingesting an already-seen event is idempotent" (the scenario where the same event ends up in two shards and `read_all` collapses it) passes vacuously on every input this strategy can produce. Two concrete notes: (1) the stated emulation of `read_all` is false — the generator cannot emit a log that needs the very de-duplication it advertises; (2) if `Event.compute_id()` is content-addressed without the agent in the hash, the missing de-duplication is worse than a no-op, because two different agents producing the same `(kind, subject, data)` at the same Lamport value would then emit two events with identical ids into a log that `read_all` would never return, and a fold comparing "live" to "replayed" would diverge. Either way, the de-duplication step the docstring promises is absent from the code.
chunk_findings.title: tests/property/evstrategies.py:event_logs (return statement, `return sorted(out, key=Event.sort_key)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The test never folds a duplicated log. `once` is `fold(_sorted_unique(events))` and the comparison is `fold(_sorted_unique(twice)) == once`, but `_sorted_unique` is exactly the sort-and-dedup union, so when it works (which is the assumption the property rests on) `_sorted_unique(twice)` is the identical list to `_sorted_unique(events)`, and the assertion collapses to `fold(Y) == fold(Y)` for Y = `_sorted_unique(events)`. Consequently the asserted property ("a log read with every event twice folds to the same State as the log read once") is not exercised: the duplicates are removed by `_sorted_unique` before `fold` ever sees them. Concretely, if `fold` were changed so that a log containing an event twice double-counts it (breaking fold-level idempotence), the test would still pass, because it only ever calls `fold` on a de-duplicated list. A test that pinned the claim would fold `twice` (the raw concatenation) and compare that to `once`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/property/test_fold_properties.py:62 (test_a_duplicated_history_folds_like_the_history_once)

chunk_findings.detail: The test cannot detect order-dependence in `fold`, which is what it is named for. `shuffled` is a permutation of `events`, so `_sorted_unique(shuffled) == _sorted_unique(events)` at line 70 is true by construction of sort+dedup and contributes nothing; and at line 71 the shuffled list is re-canonicalized by `_sorted_unique` before `fold` sees it, then compared against `fold(events)` where `event_logs()` emits a log (i.e. already in canonical order). Both sides therefore fold the same canonical list, so the assertion is `fold(X) == fold(X)`. Concretely, if `fold` were changed to aggregate strictly in the order events arrive, this test still passes because no shuffled list is ever handed to `fold`; to pin order-freeness the shuffle would have to be folded directly (`fold(shuffled) == fold(events)`), not through `_sorted_unique`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/property/test_fold_properties.py:70-71 (test_the_order_shards_are_read_in_does_not_matter)

chunk_findings.detail:
The oracle's skip rule does not implement the behaviour its own docstring describes. The docstring says an ancestor's need is exempt when it is "an umbrella's need on its own child ... met by running it -- `inherited_deps`", but the code only exempts a need whose target is inside the *offered item's* subtree (`own_subtree = descendants(item_id) | {item_id}`), so a need on an ancestor of the offered item is never exempted.

Concrete input (all events valid `task.added`s; `event_logs`/`task.added` supports arbitrary `parent`+`needs`, and the composite draws both):
- `A` parent `""`, `needs: ["C"]`
- `C` parent `"A"`, `needs: []`
- `D` parent `"C"`, `needs: []`

`plan` must offer `D` once nothing else blocks it: `inherited_deps(D)` cannot contain `C`, otherwise `C` (an umbrella, never offered itself) could only become DONE after `D` and its siblings run, while `D` waits for `C` to be DONE — a deadlock, so the scheduler necessarily exempts an ancestor's need on one of its own children/ancestors of the item. But `_deps_met(state, "D")` walks `D -> C -> A`, and at `cur = A` it sees `dep = "C"`; because `C` is an ancestor of `D`, `C not in own_subtree("D")`, so it falls through to `d.state != DONE` and returns `False`. `test_an_offer_is_never_made_before_its_dependencies` then asserts `_deps_met(state, it.id)` and fails even though the offer is legitimate — a false failure. The exemption should be based on the ancestor/path relation (a need pointing at a node whose subtree contains the offered item), not solely on the item's own descendants.
chunk_findings.title: tests/property/test_scheduler_properties.py: `_deps_met` (lines ~69–86)

data.summary: inherited_deps hands a grandchild its ancestor's need on the grandchild's own parent: A needs C, C is A's child, D is C's child -> D blocked 'C is open (inherited from A)' while C is an umbrella waiting on D: a permanent hang (the subtree exemption covers only the item's own descendants, not its ancestors between it and the need's owner)
data.title: Umbrella need on its own child deadlocks that child's sub-tasks

data.body:
Research R-compat, decision D-compat (operator 2026-10-06). Generate fixtures by installing released wheels (0.1.3, 0.1.10, 0.1.15, 0.1.18 and the current release) into throwaway venvs, building a small project with each, and committing the logs, config and adopted files. Tests: (1) new reads old: the golden folded state and replay are identical, and upgrade --apply makes every migration verify; (2) old reads new: an old wheel against a project written by the new release refuses only conflicting writes, preserves unknown parts, and never crashes; (3) surface snapshots (--help tree, tools/list, JSON schemas, config --explain, event-kind registry) are diffed against the previous release, and every difference must be declared in the manifest. The matrix runs in CI (slow marker) and in release.sh.

Split into: B-uni-compat-tests.1-fixtures, B-uni-compat-tests.2-old-reads-new, B-uni-compat-tests.3-surface, B-uni-compat-tests.4-upgrade-apply.

data.claim: ddflow releases are not on a package index, so each wheel must be built from its release commit (tags from 0.1.9, 'release X' commits before); built that way, a fixed scenario runs on 0.1.3, 0.1.10, 0.1.15, 0.1.18 and HEAD, and the current strict fold agrees with each release's own fold on every shared record field except fold bugs fixed since

chunk_findings.detail: `main` iterates `[*RELEASES, "current"]` and maps `current` to the version string declared in `ddflow/__init__.py`, then `build(declared, HEAD)` writes to `OUT / declared` after `shutil.rmtree(dest, ignore_errors=True)`. The only guard is `if declared != version: raise SystemExit(...)`, which compares two strings and therefore cannot distinguish "the wheel built from the v0.1.18 tag" from "HEAD, which still calls itself 0.1.18". Given a checkout where `__version__` is still `0.1.18` but HEAD has commits after the `v0.1.18` tag (i.e. any point in the development cycle between a release and the next version bump), running the documented no-argument command `scripts/ci/compat-matrix build` first correctly writes `tests/fixtures/releases/0.1.18/` from the tag and then immediately deletes it and rewrites it from HEAD. The result is that the `0.1.18` entry's `expected.json` was folded by the current (unreleased) wheel and its `project/` reflects unreleased code, so `tests/compat`'s "new release reads the 0.1.18 log" check becomes current-vs-current and passes vacuously, while `meta.json`'s commit no longer matches the tag the directory is named after. Because the version check only compares the declared string, this happens silently; a distinct on-disk namespace (or a check that `release_commit(declared)` equals `HEAD`) is needed.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/ci/compat-matrix: `main`/`build` (the `current` branch and `dest = OUT / version`)

chunk_findings.detail: `differences` iterates only over `expected`'s keys and never inspects keys that exist in `actual` but not in `expected`. The module docstring justifies this rule as "a field a newer release added is not a difference", but the same code path is used for the per-collection record maps produced at line 63 (`out[name] = {key: plain(records[key]) for key in sorted(records)}`) and compared at the top level. There the dict keys are record IDs, not dataclass field names, so the rule silently swallows added *records*. Concretely, with `expected = {"items": {"I-1": {...}}}` (the old release's reading) and `actual = {"items": {"I-1": {...}, "I-2": {...}}}` (the current release folded the same log into one extra item), the dict branch loops over `"items"`, recurses into the two record dicts, walks only `I-1`, and returns `[]`; the "new reads old / golden folded state identical" assertion therefore passes even though the folded states differ — exactly the class of regression this test exists to catch. Note the asymmetry: the list branch (line 78) does detect a length change, so extra set members are reported, while extra records (dict keys) are not. Iterating `actual`-only keys as "unexpected" (at least for the collection maps) would close this hole.
chunk_findings.title: tests/compat/projection.py:69-77 (`differences`, dict branch)

chunk_findings.detail: `VERSIONS` is built at import time by sorting every fixture directory name with `tuple(int(x) for x in v.split("."))`. The change's own stated intent is that `scripts/ci/compat-matrix` builds **five** projects and "commits its log, config and adopted files under tests/fixtures/releases/" — the fifth being the `current` build, whose fixture directory is not a dotted numeric version (it is the "current" entry, e.g. `tests/fixtures/releases/current/`, and any dev-style id such as `0.1.19.dev0` fails identically). For that input `int("current")` (or `int("dev0")`) raises `ValueError` during module import, so pytest fails **collection of the whole module**: neither `test_the_matrix_has_its_releases` (the guard that is supposed to detect a missing fixture) nor any of the `release`-parametrized tests run at all. The directory filter only requires a numeric-parseable name to be absent from the guard's four-version subset assertion, so nothing in the file catches this before the sort blows up. Input that demonstrates it: a committed fixture directory `tests/fixtures/releases/current/meta.json` — import of this test module raises `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'current'`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/compat/test_new_reads_old.py:37-40 (`VERSIONS` sort key)

chunk_findings.detail: The split of task `T2` into `T2.a` and `T2.b` copied the parent’s `globs` (`src/app.py`), `priority`, and `tags`, but not its `needs`. `T2` still declares `needs: ["T1"]`, and both children do work that consumes T1’s parser (`T2.a` is “Call the parser”, `T2.b` is “Report parse errors”), yet their `needs` arrays are empty. If the same split is performed while `T1` is still open (or after the open bug `B73cceded0f` invalidates `T1`), the planner will mark `T2.a`/`T2.b` ready and run them before `src/parser.py` exists, causing failures. The golden folded state should record `needs: ["T1"]` on both children.
chunk_findings.title: tests/fixtures/releases/0.1.10/expected.json:items."T2.a".needs / items."T2.b".needs

chunk_findings.detail: The `lamport` clock in this per-agent event log is not contiguous: it runs 1,2,…,31 and then jumps to 36,37,38,39 for the final four events (`task.added` T2.a, `task.added` T2.b, `task.updated` T2, `session.ended`). Events 32–35 are absent from a file that is supposed to be the complete log of a single-writer session — every line in the file carries `"agent":"fx-alice"` and there is no companion agent file referenced, so there is no writer that could have consumed 32–35. Concretely, a reader that treats `lamport` as the per-agent sequence number (which is what a "fold old log, replay must be identical" compat test needs in order to detect dropped/compacted events and to order events within the file) will either flag the hole as corruption or place `T2.a`, `T2.b`, the `T2` update and the session end at positions 36–39 while the committed golden folded state was produced with them at 32–35, making replay differ from the golden. If the intent was simply that these last four events follow `bug.found`, they should carry `lamport` 32, 33, 34, 35; the stored values 36–39 are an off-by-four drift.
chunk_findings.title: tests/fixtures/releases/0.1.10/project/.ddflow/events/fx-alice.jsonl (lines 31→32)

chunk_findings.detail: This is presented as the raw per-agent log produced by 0.1.15, but fx-alice's own Lamport counter is not contiguous. The `ddflow.seen` event on line 1 has `lamport:1`, and lines 2–33 run 2,3,4,…,33 with no gaps, i.e. this agent's counter starts at 1 and increments by exactly one per event it writes. It then jumps 33 → 39: the `task.added` for `T2.a` carries `lamport:39`, `T2.b` carries 40, and the `task.updated` for `T2` carries 41, while the wall clock shows a ~2.5 s gap between `…T13:05:00.069313Z` (lamport 33) and `…T13:05:02.599386Z` (lamport 39). Five events (34–38) that the same agent actually consumed sequence numbers for are missing from the committed file, so the fixture is a filtered/edited capture rather than the append-only log the tests claim to replay. Consequence: a golden folded state captured from the live 0.1.15 run (or any reader that relies on this agent's Lamport stream being complete, e.g. a high-water-mark or sequencer check) will not be reproduced by replaying this file, and if any of the dropped events mutated folded state (split bookkeeping, gate, lease, prompt) the "replay identical" assertion can pass against a fixture that silently omits those transitions.

chunk_findings.detail:
`parse` calls `line.rstrip('\n')` on lines produced by `text.splitlines()`, which by definition have no terminator attached, so the call is a no-op. This is not a behavioral defect (the output is identical either way), so I do not consider it a reportable correctness issue — noting only to explain why it is not being raised further.

After reviewing the diff, I find no input, interleaving, or environment in which these fixture files produce wrong behavior. The two files are inert test inputs: `app.main()` returns the constant `0`, and `parser.parse` maps `"a,b\nc,d"` to `[["a","b"],["c","d"]]`, which is the expected folding input for the compat-matrix test described in the intent. Nothing in the added code is executable at import time, mutates global state, or depends on the environment.
chunk_findings.title: tests/fixtures/releases/0.1.3/project/src/parser.py

chunk_findings.detail: The committed golden fixture embeds the author's workstation launcher path `/home/delian/src/ddflow/.venv/bin/ddflow` in the `UserPromptSubmit` hook command. Two problems follow. First, it contradicts the documented procedure: the intent says each release wheel is installed into a *throwaway* venv and the sample project is built "with each" wheel, so `ddflow hooks install --claude` run by the release binary should have recorded the throwaway venv's path (or, after that venv is deleted, nothing resolvable). Recording the developer's working-copy dev venv means the fixture was produced by the dev install, not by the 0.2.0 wheel — so the golden "folded/adopted state" for 0.2.0 reflects whatever unreleased code was in `/home/delian/src/ddflow`, not the tagged commit `a0d87d894328dfdde10db0af020c8f9fc74827d8` named in `meta.json`. Second, the file is machine-specific: on any other machine (CI included) that absolute path does not exist, the hook silently degrades to the `command -v ddflow` / "not found" branch, and re-running the documented fixture script cannot reproduce this file byte-for-byte (the path changes with `$HOME`/venv location). Any assertion that the golden fixture matches a replay, or that it is regenerable, will differ on every machine except the author's. The path should be normalized (e.g. to the throwaway venv pattern or a placeholder) before committing.

chunk_findings.detail: When HEAD's declared `__version__` equals a version that is also in `RELEASES` — exactly the state the file's own docstring tells you to create ("rebuild it when a release is cut, and add the release to RELEASES") — the default run `compat-matrix build` iterates `[*RELEASES, "current"]`, i.e. it builds the tagged release *first* and the HEAD build *last*. `build` does `dest = OUT / version; shutil.rmtree(dest, ignore_errors=True)`, so the `current` iteration computes `declared` from `ddflow/__init__.py`, gets e.g. `"0.1.18"`, and (because `version` for the current build *is* `declared`, the `if declared != version` guard can never fire for it) writes onto `tests/fixtures/releases/0.1.18/`, deleting the fixture that was just generated from tag `v0.1.18` and replacing `meta.json`'s `commit` with HEAD, plus a `project/` and `expected.json` produced by the newer tree. The release fixture is gone, and the "new reads old" test for 0.1.18 now compares current code against current code, which is tautological. Demonstrated by: a checkout whose `ddflow/__init__.py` still says `__version__ = "0.1.18"` (the tagged release commit is `v0.1.18`), then `scripts/ci/compat-matrix build`; the script prints both `0.1.18: tests/fixtures/releases/0.1.18 (…)` lines and the second rmtree wipes the first. Nothing rejects `current` colliding with a `RELEASES` entry, and the order guarantees the clobber.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/ci/compat-matrix (main → build, `dest = OUT / version`)

chunk_findings.detail: `differences` only ever iterates `expected.keys()` and recursively descends into keys that are present in `actual`; keys that exist in `actual` but not in `expected` are never looked at, at *any* depth. The docstring justifies this as "a field a newer release added is not a difference", but record *collections* (`items`, `bugs`, `sessions`, ...) are ordinary dicts too, so the same rule makes newly-added **records** invisible. Concretely: `differences({"items": {"a": 1}}, {"items": {"a": 1, "b": 2}})` returns `[]`. In the real test this means a regression where the current release folds one extra record out of the same event log (e.g. an event applied twice, or an event now materialised as an extra item) produces `actual` with an extra key under `items`, `differences` returns empty, and the "new reads old / replay identical" assertion passes even though the new reading is not identical to the golden one. `event_count` (line 61) does not save you here, because the number of events read is unchanged — only the number of folded records differs. The comparison needs to check actual-only keys at the collection level (or compare lengths per collection) for the test to actually detect added records.
chunk_findings.title: tests/compat/projection.py:72 (`differences`, dict branch)

chunk_findings.detail: The scalar fallback is `[] if expected == actual else [...]`, so JSON values that are distinct but compare equal are silently treated as identical: `differences({"x": 1}, {"x": True})` returns `[]` (since `1 == True`), and `differences({"x": 1}, {"x": 1.0})` returns `[]` (since `1 == 1.0`). A fixture field that flips between numeric `0`/`1` and boolean `false`/`true`, or between an int and a float, is therefore not reported even though the golden JSON contains a different token. A type-aware comparison (`type(expected) is type(actual) and expected == actual`, or comparing the canonical `json.dumps` of each side) would catch these.
chunk_findings.title: tests/compat/projection.py:84 (`differences`, scalar fallback)

chunk_findings.detail: `VERSIONS` is computed at import time as `sorted((p.name for p in RELEASES.iterdir() if (p / "meta.json").is_file()), key=lambda v: tuple(int(x) for x in v.split(".")))`. Every fixture directory whose name is not a dot-separated list of integers makes the key function raise `ValueError`. The change description says `scripts/ci/compat-matrix` builds and commits a project for `(0.1.3, 0.1.10, 0.1.15, 0.1.18, current)` "with each and commits its log, config and adopted files under `tests/fixtures/releases/`" — so a directory named `current` (or any dev-style name such as `0.2.0.dev0`, where `int("dev0")` also raises) is expected to live next to the four release dirs. Given that input, `int("current")` raises during module import, i.e. at pytest collection, *before* `test_the_matrix_has_its_releases` can run. The result is not a clean "fixture missing" failure from the guard test the module was designed around, but a collection error that takes down the entire `tests/compat` module (every parametrized `release` test plus the "new reads old" checks) with an unhandled `ValueError`. The sort key needs to tolerate non-numeric directory names (or non-release directories need to be excluded), otherwise the very fixture the matrix is documented to produce prevents the suite from being collected.

chunk_findings.detail: The tail of this fixture is not emitted by the same log as the rest, and it is internally inconsistent. Every event in the file carries `"agent":"fx-alice"` (the only writer — the `gpt-fixture` entries at lines 20–21 are only gate *reviewers* recorded by fx-alice), so this agent's `lamport` counter must be contiguous: line 31 has `lamport:31`, and the next event, `task.added` for `T2.a`, jumps to `lamport:36` (then 37, 38, 39). Events with lamports 32–35 are absent from the only log that could contain them. The same four tail events also use a different payload shape: the `task.added` events at lines 32–33 (`T2.a`, `T2.b`) omit `"body"`, `"line"` and `"tags"`, which *every* other `task.added` in this same file (`T1`/`T2`/`T3`, lines 2–4) carries explicitly as `""`/`""`/`[]`. Given that `tests/compat` folds this log and compares it to the golden state, four missing events mean the folded state cannot equal a state produced by the real 0.1.10 run (the `T2` split at line 34, the bug at line 31, etc. are reconstructed on top of a hole in the lamport sequence), and any reducer that indexes `data["tags"]`/`data["body"]` on a `task.added` payload — as the old-format events earlier in this very file teach it to — will `KeyError` on the `T2.a`/`T2.b` events. The tail should either be a contiguous continuation of fx-alice's own log with the release's payload schema, or the log should be complete; as written it is neither a faithful 0.1.10 log nor a well-formed one.

chunk_findings.detail: The committed fixture bakes in a machine-specific launcher path: the hook command runs `/home/delian/src/ddflow/.venv/bin/ddflow hooks prompt` and only falls back to `command -v ddflow` if that exact file is not executable. The intent states these fixtures are produced by `scripts/ci/compat-matrix` building the release commit (meta.json claims commit `0a67552…`, version 0.1.15, Python 3.12.3) into a *throwaway* venv and letting that build adopt the project — so `hooks install --claude` should have recorded the throwaway venv's launcher path, not the maintainer's private dev checkout. Two concrete consequences: (a) any compat test that replays this folded state and actually invokes the recorded hook on CI (where neither `/home/delian/src/ddflow/.venv/bin/ddflow` nor a `ddflow` on `PATH` exists) silently degrades to the "ddflow: not found … this check was skipped" branch, so the `UserPromptSubmit` check under test never runs; (b) any test that regenerates the fixture and compares it (or diffs it against freshly adopted output on another machine/venv) cannot match, because the generated string will contain that machine's venv path instead. This is the same class of leak the neighbouring `.ddflow/.gitignore` explicitly warns about for `reviewers.toml` ("a LAN endpoint committed here reaches every clone") — the fixture should record a normalized or placeholder launcher path, or the path of the built wheel's venv.

They run 1,2,…,33 and then jump to 39,40,41,42 (`fix-B2f2148b33b` at lamport 33, `T2.a` at lamport 39; 5 values — 34–38 — are absent). Since this is the only file in which fx-alice's events can live (the other records in the file are fx-alice's own gate/session/worktree events, and no second agent appears anywhere in the stream), those five events are simply missing from the captured "log" the change claims to commit. Concretely: folding/replaying this file yields a state built from only 37 events, whereas the golden folded state committed alongside the fixture was produced from the full run; the `34–38` slice sits exactly between `bug.found B2f2148b33b` (32) / `task.added fix-B2f2148b33b` (33) and the `T2` split (39–41), i.e. it is precisely the region where the fix task's state and the split's intermediate state would be recorded, so a golden-vs-replay comparison can mismatch. If the intent is a faithful replay fixture, the capture step is dropping events (or the file is corrupt); either way it is not a complete `fx-alice` log.

chunk_findings.detail: `T2` ("Wire the parser into the app") carries `"needs": ["T1"]` and its body records `"Split into: T2.a, T2.b."`. The two split children created at `2026-10-07T13:05:03.917/918` inherit essentially every other attribute of the parent — `"parent": "T2"`, `"globs": ["src/app.py"]`, `priority: 100`, `base`, `branch`, `kind` — but both come out with `"needs": []`. Since this file is the golden folded state that `tests/compat` asserts against for the 0.1.18 log (new code reads old data, "golden folded state and replay identical"), the fixture bakes in the loss of the dependency: any consumer that schedules from this state will treat `T2.a` "Call the parser" as unblocked and can hand it out before `T1` ("Write the parser") has landed, which is exactly the ordering `T2` declared with `needs: ["T1"]`. The fixture cannot catch this itself, because at split time `T1` happens to be already `"done"` (`completed_at 2026-10-07T13:04:59.822973Z`, ahead of the 13:05:03 split), so no comparison of golden-vs-folded ever observes the missing `needs`; the defect only manifests when the same fold is replayed/scheduled with `T1` still open (e.g. `T1` reopened, or the log truncated before the merge gate at 13:04:59).

chunk_findings.detail: Every event in this 37-line file is attributed to the single agent `fx-alice` and to the single session `s20261007T130451-1220344` (`ddflow.seen` sets `agent:"fx-alice"`, `lease.acquired.holder` is `fx-alice`, all gates `by` are `fx-alice`/`gpt-fixture`, and there is no second session or worktree in the log). In such a single-writer stream, the lamport clock must advance by exactly one per event, and it does so for the first 33 events (1,2,…,33). It then jumps: the `task.added` for `T2.a` is `"lamport":39`, `T2.b` is 40, `task.updated` `T2` is 41, `session.ended` is 42 — lamports 34–38 are simply absent, with no events anywhere in this file carrying them. The timestamps confirm a ~2.6 s hole between the `fix-Bc0bfa67558` `task.added` (13:05:01.284786, lamport 33) and `T2.a` (13:05:03.917301, lamport 39), so five events were generated and then dropped from the recorded log. The failure mode: this directory is a *golden* release fixture whose stated purpose is that the new code "reads old (golden folded state and replay identical)". Replaying this log can only reconstruct the state that exists after lamport 33 plus the four tail events, so if any of the five missing events (whatever they did in that 2.6 s window — note the split of `T2` is only recorded as the `body` of `task.updated` at lamport 41) touched folded state (config/adopted or task status), the replayed fold will not equal the committed golden state, and `tests/compat` will fail nondeterministically depending on whether the golden was produced from the full run or from this truncated file. Either the five events were lost, or the tail events were written with lamports offset by +5; both make the fixture internally inconsistent and unusable as a replay reference.

chunk_findings.detail: The recorded `UserPromptSubmit` hook command embeds the absolute path `/home/delian/src/ddflow/.venv/bin/ddflow` — the maintainer's in-repo development virtualenv. The stated build procedure is to build each release wheel into a *throwaway* venv and build the sample project with that venv, so a hook installed by that procedure would record the throwaway venv's path (e.g. `/tmp/.../bin/ddflow`) or a PATH-based command, never `/home/delian/src/ddflow/.venv`. This means the fixture's golden `.claude/settings.json` did not capture what release 0.2.0 produces; it captured a hook that was left over from the developer's own checkout (or a live install on that machine). Any compat assertion that compares the fixture's adopted `settings.json` to what `ddflow hooks install --claude`/`adopt` emits — or that re-runs `adopt` and diffs — will diverge on any machine other than this one, and the fixture silently skips exercising the release's own installer path. Concretely: on CI the hook would read `/home/runner/work/.../venv/bin/ddflow` (or `command -v ddflow`), not the recorded path, so a golden comparison of this file fails there while passing on the maintainer's box, or conversely passes without ever validating the release's install behavior.

chunk_findings.detail: This file is a per-agent event log: every event carries `"agent":"fx-alice"`, and the Lamport counter for this agent runs contiguously 1,2,3,…,32,33 — one increment per event, starting at 1 — through the `bug.found`/`fix-B731d9175e6` pair. chunk_findings.detail: The five events carry `lamport` 34–38 but timestamps `2026-10-07T13:47:03`–`13:47:04`. This shard is the one the author's triage uses to "refute" the earlier finding that the 0.1.18 `fx-alice.jsonl` log jumps straight from `lamport:33` to `lamport:39` with values 34–38 missing ("Lamport is one clock across all shards, not per agent: the gap is fx-bob, whose shard holds exactly the missing values"). chunk_findings.detail:
The file declares 0.1.3's `decision list` as a known, tolerated failure (`OWN_BUGS[("0.1.3", "decision list")] = "KeyError: 'live'"`, introduced precisely "so a fixed or unrelated failure is told apart"), but the tolerance branch is guarded by an unconditional no-traceback assertion that runs first:

```python
code, out, err = old.run(*argv)
assert "Traceback" not in err + out, (err + out)[-1500:]   # <-- fires first
own = OWN_BUGS.get((old.version, " ".join(argv)))
if own:
    assert code == 1 and own in err + out, (code, out, err)
    return
```

The declared message `KeyError: 'live'` is exactly the repr line Python writes at the end of a traceback for an uncaught exception. With input `old.version == "0.1.3"`, `argv == ("decision", "list")` on a project that contains a decision, the command dies with an uncaught `KeyError`, so stderr contains `Traceback (most recent call last):` and the exit code is 1. The very first assertion therefore fails and the test errors out, and the `code == 1 and own in err + out` check (plus the tolerance `return`) is never reached. So the case the test author explicitly declared as acceptable makes the test red, and the mechanism that was supposed to "tell a fixed or unrelated failure apart" is dead for the one failure it was written for. Moving the `OWN_BUGS` lookup (or the no-traceback assertion) so the declared case short-circuits before the blanket check fixes it. The sibling non-own check `assert not re.search(r"^\w*Error\b", ...)` further shows the author knew to exempt this message from the generic error scan but not from the traceback scan.

chunk_findings.detail:
The filter that is meant to drop git's private directory also drops every project file whose path component merely *contains* the substring `.git`: `p.relative_to(self.root).parts` is a tuple of path components, and `".git" in (".ddflow", ".gitignore")` is `True` because `".gitignore"` contains `".git"`. So `.ddflow/.gitignore` (and `.gitattributes`, `.gitkeep`, `.github/...`) are never put into the returned dict — they are invisible to both `before` and `after`.

Concrete consequence: `ADOPT_OVERWRITES["0.1.3"]` and `ADOPT_OVERWRITES["0.1.10"]` both contain `".ddflow/.gitignore"`, but `_changed` is computed purely from the keys of `before`/`after`, so `changed` can never contain `".ddflow/.gitignore"`. `test_old_adopt_over_newer_managed_files` ends with `assert changed == ADOPT_OVERWRITES[old.version]`, which therefore always fails for 0.1.3 and 0.1.10 (expected set has 3 entries, one of which is unreachable) — regardless of what the release actually rewrites. Symmetrically, `test_old_write_preserves_what_it_does_not_understand` / `test_old_reads_the_newer_project` get a false pass: a release that rewrites `.ddflow/.gitignore` during a read or a write still satisfies `_changed(old, before) == set()`, contradicting the "leave every byte that was already there untouched" contract the file claims to pin. The intended check is a component equality (e.g. `".git" not in p.relative_to(self.root).parts` replaced by rejecting only the exact `.git` part, as in `".git" not in p.parts[:1]` / `p.parts[0] != ".git"`).

chunk_findings.detail: The guard `assert not re.search(r"re\.(split|findall)\(r?[\"']\\W", source)` only matches call sites whose regex literal begins with an *uppercase* `\W` immediately after the quote. Two far more common spellings of a word splitter slip through: `re.findall(r"\w+", text)` (lowercase `w`; regex matching is case-sensitive) and `re.findall(r"[\w-]+", text.lower())` (the `-` variant needed for the `hyphens=True`/rules path), since the character after the quote is `[` / `w`, not `\W`. A precompiled splitter such as `_TOKEN = re.compile(r"[\w-]+")` plus `_TOKEN.findall(text)` is missed for a different reason: the pattern requires `re.(split|findall)(`, so `re.compile(...)` never matches. This matters because the GOLDEN test only pins *behaviour*, and behaviour is byte-identical by design (that is the whole point of the slice), so this assertion is the only thing enforcing the stated guarantee "the callers that used to spell their own now call `textsim.words`". Concrete failure: leave `ddflow/services/rules.py` with its own `re.findall(r"[\w-]+", text.lower())` (or a module-level `re.compile`), and the entire suite still passes even though a second splitter remains behind. The assertion needs to also cover `\w`, `[...\w...]`, and `re.compile` forms (or, better, assert the callers actually delegate to `textsim.words`).

chunk_findings.detail:
```python
with pytest.raises(tomllib.TOMLDecodeError):
    _toml_upsert("[a\nx = 1\n", "a.y", "1")
```

The writer under test (`_toml_upsert`, now backed by tomlkit) surfaces the parser's error type, and tomlkit does not raise `tomllib.TOMLDecodeError`: its parser raises `tomlkit.exceptions.ParseError` (a `ValueError` subclass), which is unrelated to the stdlib `tomllib.TOMLDecodeError`. Given the input `"[a\nx = 1\n"` (an unterminated `[a` table header), the call in the `pytest.raises(...)` block propagates `tomlkit.exceptions.ParseError`, not `tomllib.TOMLDecodeError`; `pytest.raises` performs an `isinstance` check, so it will not match and the test fails even though a parse error *was* raised. The test name ("reported as toml does") asserts a stdlib-`tomllib` exception contract that the tomlkit-based `_toml_upsert` does not provide, so this assertion is wrong for the implementation it is testing.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_config_writer.py :: test_text_that_is_not_toml_is_reported_as_toml_does

chunk_findings.detail: A `dotted` path with no dot (a legitimate top-level TOML key, e.g. `name`, `version`) is mishandled. `section, _, key = dotted.rpartition(".")` yields `section == ""`, and `[p.strip() for p in "".split(".")]` yields `[""]`, not `[]`. The loop therefore treats `""` as a section name: with `upsert("", "enabled", "true")` the document is empty so `doc.add(...)` is skipped, then `doc[""] = tomlkit.table()` is executed and `enabled` is written *inside* an empty-named table, producing `[""]\nenabled = true` (or, if tomlkit rejects the empty key, a `ValueError` via the `except` path since `tomllib.loads("")` succeeds). Either way the top-level key is never set. The docstring only promises `<section>.<key>` support, but nothing rejects/guards the no-dot form, so the first caller that passes a bare key silently corrupts the file instead of raising.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/tomlcfg.py:upsert

chunk_findings.detail: `_LITERAL = re.compile(r"(true|false|-?\d+(\.\d+)?|\[.*\]|\{.*\})")` matches digit strings that are *not* valid TOML numbers, because it accepts arbitrary leading zeros. `literal("01234")` returns `"01234"` unchanged (bare), and `upsert(text, "a.id", "01234")` then does `tomlkit.parse("v = 01234")`, which fails (TOML forbids leading zeros); the `except TOMLKitError` branch runs `tomllib.loads(text)` (succeeds for valid `text`) and raises `ValueError("cannot set 'a.id' to '01234'")`. So a user who runs the CLI with a value like `--set id 01234` (zip code, zero-padded ID) gets an error instead of the string `"01234"`, even though the documented contract is "itself when it already is a boolean, a number, an array or an inline table" — `01234` is none of those. The same loose patterns let `[a b]` / `{a}` through as "arrays"/"inline tables" and fail the same way.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/tomlcfg.py:literal

chunk_findings.detail: The test feeds invalid TOML (`"[a\nx = 1\n"`) to `_toml_upsert` and asserts `pytest.raises(tomllib.TOMLDecodeError)`. But this change makes `_toml_upsert` a tomlkit-backed editor (`configwrite`'s hand-built parser is replaced by "tomlkit editing in place"), and tomlkit's parser does not raise `tomllib.TOMLDecodeError`. It raises `tomlkit.exceptions.ParseError` (which subclasses `ValueError`/`TOMLKitError`, not `TOMLDecodeError`). Since `ParseError` is not a subclass of `TOMLDecodeError`, `pytest.raises(tomllib.TOMLDecodeError)` will not catch it; pytest re-raises the unexpected exception and the test errors instead of passing. The test therefore only passes if `_toml_upsert` additionally wraps tomlkit errors into `TOMLDecodeError`, which nothing in the stated design does.

chunk_findings.detail: `literal()` documents its contract as "``text`` as a TOML value: itself when it already is a boolean, a number, an array or an inline table … else a quoted, escaped string", but `_LITERAL = (true|false|-?(0|[1-9]\d*)(\.\d+)?|\[.*\]|\{.*\})` only recognises decimal integers and plain `d.d` decimals. Every other TOML number form is silently downgraded to text: `literal("1e6")` returns `'"1e6"'`, `literal("0x1F")` returns `'"0x1F"'`, `literal("+1")` returns `'"+1"'`, `literal("1_000")` returns `'"1_000"'` (also `inf`/`nan`/octal/binary). So `--set timeout 1e6` (or any caller of `literal` in `commands/review._toml_value` / `Rule.to_toml`) writes `timeout = "1e6"` — a string where the user typed a number — contradicting the function's own stated behaviour and changing the value's type in the written config. The regex should at least cover the TOML float/integer forms it claims to accept, or the docstring must stop promising "a number".
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/tomlcfg.py :: `_LITERAL` / `literal()`

chunk_findings.detail: The test wraps a direct call to `configwrite._toml_upsert` (imported at the top of this file from `ddflow.services.configwrite`) in `pytest.raises(tomllib.TOMLDecodeError)`. The triage declaring this refuted points at error conversion "in tomlcfg.upsert except branch" — a different callable in a different module. The test never passes through `tomlcfg.upsert` unless `configwrite._toml_upsert` explicitly delegates to it, and nothing in the diff or the probe establishes that delegation; the function is described here as "backed by tomlkit", i.e. handing text to tomlkit's parser. For the input `"[a\nx = 1\n"` (unterminated `[a` header), tomlkit's parser raises `tomlkit.exceptions.ParseError`, which is a `ValueError` sibling of — not a subclass of — `tomllib.TOMLDecodeError`, so `pytest.raises(tomllib.TOMLDecodeError)` fails on the mismatched exception type. The probe therefore does not answer the finding for the call site actually exercised: the assertion only holds if `configwrite._toml_upsert` itself re-raises as `tomllib.TOMLDecodeError`, which this diff does not show.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_config_writer.py :: test_text_that_is_not_toml_is_reported_as_toml_does

chunk_findings.detail:
When `dotted` contains no dot, `parts` is `[]`, so the loop is skipped and the value is set directly on the document with `table[key.strip()] = value`. tomlkit's `Container.__setitem__`/`add` appends a new key to the **end** of the document body, i.e. after every existing `[section]` header and its keys. A key that appears textually after a `[header]` is, by TOML's rules, part of that table — so the "top level" key is silently written into the last section instead of the root. Concrete input: `text = "[review]
enabled = false
"`, `upsert(text, "name", '"x"')` returns `"[review]
enabled = false
name = "x"
"`, which re‑parses as `review.name == "x"` and has no top‑level `name`. This directly contradicts the contract finding #1 was fixed for ("A `dotted` path with no dot … is a top‑level TOML key") and the function's own docstring; the probe only exercises the empty‑document case (`upsert("", "enabled", "true")`), where there is no preceding table, so it cannot catch this. Note the code already has special handling for new *sections* at the document root (`doc.add(tomlkit.nl())` before creating a top‑level table, which is correct because a new header at the end is still top level), but nothing ensures a new root‑level *key* is inserted before the first table the way TOML requires.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/tomlcfg.py `upsert` (the `table[key.strip()] = value` path when `parts == []`)

chunk_findings.detail: This hunk adds `{ name = "tomlkit" }` to the project's resolved `dependencies` list and `{ name = "tomlkit", specifier = ">=0.13" }` to `[package.metadata] requires-dist`, but does not add a corresponding `[[package]]` entry for tomlkit anywhere in `uv.lock` (it must carry `name`, `version`, `source`, and `sdist`/`wheels` with hashes — none of the three file's hunks introduce such a block). Every package named in a lock's dependency lists must have a resolved `[[package]]` record, so with this file `uv sync --frozen` / `uv lock --check` / `uv run --frozen` fails with "The lockfile at `uv.lock` needs to be updated, but `--frozen` was provided", and any environment pinned to the checked-in lock cannot install the newly declared runtime dependency that the rest of this change (the tomlkit-backed TOML writer) depends on. This is the observed symptom of hand-editing the two metadata lists instead of regenerating the lock with `uv lock`, which would have emitted the `[[package]] tomlkit` block with its wheel/sdist hashes. (If tomlkit were already resolved in the lock as a transitive/dev package at a version satisfying `>=0.13`, this hunk would be complete and the finding would not apply; given the project's declared deps — jinja2, model2vec, rapidfuzz, sqlite-vec, watchfiles, mcp-sdk — none of which pulls tomlkit, a pre-existing entry is not expected.)

chunk_findings.detail: The fixture inserts `b`, then `a` (removed), then `c`, so the surviving items are `b, c` — which is *also* their lexicographic order. The assertions `[i.id for i in st.live_items()] == ["b", "c"]` and `list(st.live_by_id()) == ["b", "c"]` therefore pass for any implementation that returns live items sorted by id, not just one that preserves dict/definition order. Concretely, if `State.live_items()` were changed to `sorted(self.items.values(), key=lambda i: i.id)` (or `live_by_id` to a sorted dict), every assertion in this test — including the alias check `st.live_by_id()["b"] is st.items["b"]` — still passes green, so the property "keeps definition order" is unverified. Inserting the items as `c, a(removed), b` would make live order `["c", "b"] != sorted ["b", "c"]` and actually test the claim.

chunk_findings.detail: `_count` runs `re.findall` over the raw text of every `ddflow/**/*.py`, so it counts occurrences in comments and docstrings, and it only matches one exact spelling. Two concrete consequences: (a) adding the literal text `(DONE, ABANDONED)` in a comment or docstring anywhere in `ddflow/` raises the count and can trip `test_terminal_spellings_only_go_down` even though no real spelled-out site exists; (b) a genuine spelled-out site written in an equivalent form the regex does not cover — e.g. `if s.state in {DONE, ABANDONED}:` (set literal) or an early-return loop `for it in state.items.values(): if not it.removed:` — is never counted, so the promised guard "only goes down" can be satisfied while the invariant it is meant to protect is violated. The regex matches the textual form, not the behaviour, so it is neither sufficient (evadable spellings) nor specific (comments count).

chunk_findings.detail: `gate_satisfied` dispatches to `GateOutcome.settled(...)`, but the method's own docstring says "See `GateOutcome.satisfies`", and the stated intent of this change is that `GateOutcome` gains `satisfies(required)` "as the single definition of a settled gate". Two of the three references to the enum method (`satisfies` in the intent, `satisfies` in the docstring) disagree with the one thing the code actually calls (`settled`). If part 1 defines the method under the intended name `satisfies`, then this line raises `AttributeError: type object 'GateOutcome' has no attribute 'settled'` for every call site added by this diff: `completion.py` (`missing = [... not it.gate_satisfied(g, True)]`), `services/gates/outcomes.py` (`settled = {g: it.gate_satisfied(g, g in required) ...}`), and `views/markdown.py` (`todo = [... not it.gate_satisfied(...)]`). Concretely, the first call to `Item.gate_satisfied("design", True)` on any item — e.g. building the brief's gates-remaining in markdown.py — fails at import/call time, so the whole gate-status/brief/completion path is broken, not merely the intended "skipped required gate" fix. Either the call must use `GateOutcome.satisfies` (matching the docstring/intent) or the enum method and docstring must be renamed consistently; as written the reviewed code is internally inconsistent and, under the change's own stated naming, non-functional.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/records.py:344 (`Item.gate_satisfied`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new method resolves the outcome through `GateOutcome.settled(self.gate_outcome(gate), required)`, but `settled` is not the API this change introduces. The intent states the enum exposes `satisfies(required)` as "the single definition of a settled gate", and the method's own docstring in this same hunk points readers at `` `GateOutcome.satisfies` ``. Nothing in the diff defines, imports or documents a `GateOutcome.settled`; if the enum only has `satisfies` (as the intent says), then `GateOutcome.settled` is an `AttributeError` on the class object, raised on the very first call. Because every consumer now funnels through this method — `Item.gate_satisfied` is called by `services/gates/outcomes.py` (`status`), `services/completion.py` (`verdict`), and `views/markdown.py` (gates-remaining) — the failure is not confined to one screen: e.g. rendering the brief for any item with a pipeline (`pipeline_for` returns a non-empty list, so `settled = {g: it.gate_satisfied(...) ...}` is evaluated) raises `AttributeError: type object 'GateOutcome' has no attribute 'settled'` instead of producing a status. The call should go through the member method, e.g. `GateOutcome(self.gate_outcome(gate)).satisfies(required)`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/records.py:344 (`Item.gate_satisfied`)

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts `"verify": completion` for every parametrisation, i.e. it claims `verify._gates` already answers the unified "does this gate stop the item" question (`_completion_ok`), including the required+skipped case. But the change header states "verify.py is routed in a follow-up (held by another lane)", and the test's own comment ("Five call sites each had their own test of whether a gate's outcome is enough ... `verify._gates`") concedes that `_gates` carries its own, not-yet-unified logic. Concretely, for the parametrisation `outcome="skipped", required=True` the expectation is `completion = _completion_ok("skipped", True) = bool("skipped") and (not True or "skipped" == "passed") = False`, so the test requires `verify._gates(...).status not in {"ok", "warn"}`. An un-routed `_gates` that treats "skipped" as an accepted outcome (note `OUTCOME_EXIT["skipped"] == 0`, i.e. success) will return `ok`/`warn`, producing `"verify": True` and failing the assertion. The same holds for any required non-`passed` outcome that `_gates` historically accepted. So this change lands a test that pins the post-follow-up semantics of a module the change deliberately leaves untouched, which is a red test on this revision (or, worse, it silently coerces the follow-up lane into an expectation they did not agree to). The verify entry should either be dropped from the expectation until `verify.py` is actually routed, or the routing must land in the same change.

chunk_findings.detail: `_exit_literals` only inspects `ast.Assign` nodes and only counts a site when *every* value in the assignment is an int constant, so several ordinary ways of writing an exit code literal slip through. Demonstration: add `EXIT_FOO: int = 5` (an `ast.AnnAssign`, never matched) to e.g. `ddflow/services/export/query.py`, or `EXIT_OK, EXIT_USAGE = 0, "usage"` (tuple whose values are not all ints, so `all(...)` is false); in both cases `_exit_literals()` returns exactly the same list as before and `assert len(sites) <= OLD_EXIT_LITERALS` still passes. The comment claims the guard counts int-literal exit definitions ("the ratchet only goes down"), and the test name says codes "are defined once", but a developer can add a fresh local `EXIT_* = <int>` in either form and the ratchet will not fire. The `<= 1` slack compounds this: the test never pins *which* single site is allowed to remain, so the surviving literal can be silently substituted for a newly introduced one.

chunk_findings.detail: The previous finding #1 was "the scan is blind to ordinary spellings of an exit-code literal"; the fix extends `_pairs`/`_exit_literals` to `ast.AnnAssign` and to partially-int tuples, but the scan still only unpacks `ast.Tuple` targets, never `ast.List` targets. List-unpacking is legal Python for exactly this shape: `ast.parse("[OK, X] = 0, 'x'")` yields an `ast.Assign` whose `targets[0]` is `ast.List`, and `_pairs` falls into the `else` branch and yields `(List, Tuple)`, which fails `isinstance(t, ast.Name)`. So a module that reintroduces `[OK, UNAVAILABLE] = 0, 2` (or `[EXIT_FOO, X] = 5, 'x'`) defines the exit codes and `_exit_literals()` returns no site for it, `test_exit_codes_are_defined_once` still passes, and the new `test_the_exit_literal_scan_sees_every_spelling` does not catch it because none of its four parametrized lines uses a list target — despite its name claiming to see "every spelling". The fix answers the two exact tuple/annotation samples but not the general blindness it was raised about.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_outcome_vocabulary.py `_pairs` / `_exit_literals` (the `isinstance(target, ast.Tuple)` branch)

chunk_findings.detail: `_is_int` is `isinstance(node, ast.Constant) and isinstance(node.value, int)`, but `bool` is a subclass of `int` in Python, so `_is_int` returns `True` for `ast.Constant(value=True/False)`. Demonstration: feeding the scanner a module containing `OK = True` (or `UNAVAILABLE = False`) yields `["mod.py:1"]`, i.e. the scan reports a non-integer boolean flag as a duplicated exit-code literal and can inflate `OLD_EXIT_LITERALS`, while the function's name and the test's premise say it is detecting *int* literals. The mixed-target alternative is also inconsistent in the other direction. A guard `not isinstance(node.value, bool)` (or `type(node.value) is int`) is needed for `_is_int` to mean what it claims.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_outcome_vocabulary.py `_is_int` (line ~210)

The docstring's promise ("the message is masked either way") holds only for shapes the built-in defaults happen to know; nothing logs or surfaces that the project's own masks were dropped, and the new `test_failure_messages_fall_back_to_the_defaults_on_a_broken_config` asserts only the built-in `HOME`/`ADDR` masks, so it cannot distinguish the fallback from the old no-config code — it passes against the pre-change implementation as long as it does not crash.

chunk_findings.detail: The guard covers only `Config.load`; the line that actually consumes config-derived data — `redactor("upstream", cfg).text(str(exc)).text` — is outside it. Before this change `_safe` could not fail, because it only stringified an exception and ran the built-in profile. Now it feeds project-controlled pattern strings into the redactor from inside an already-active `except` clause, so any config that `Config.load` accepts but the redactor cannot use raises (e.g. `re.error` for `[session]\nredact_extra = ["("]` in `.ddflow/config.toml` — syntactically valid TOML, uncompilable regex; a non-list value such as `redact_extra = "ZZ-[0-9]+"` would similarly surface as a `TypeError`/`AttributeError` if the loader does not coerce it), and that new exception is raised *while handling* the original failure. Concretely, with `write_report` raising `OSError`, `prepare` enters `except (ValueError, OSError)`, calls `_safe(exc, root)`, the redactor constructor raises, and the handler propagates out of `prepare` instead of returning `Outcome("failed", FAILED, <redacted>, digest)` — the same for the `gh.Unavailable`/`gh.GhError` handlers in the send path. The failure-reporting path therefore trades "never leaks" for "can crash", which is not covered by either new test (the broken-config test only exercises `TOMLDecodeError`, which the tuple does catch).

chunk_findings.detail:
`Param.schema()` honors `choices` when `schema_enum=True` (it emits `"enum": [...]`), but `Command.input_schema()` never reaches that code: it calls `self.properties()`, which collapses each `Param` to the lossy `(type, help, required)` tuple via `spec()`, and then `properties_schema()` rebuilds a *fresh* `Param(n, type=t, help=d)` with `choices` and `schema_enum` left at their defaults. The result is that a param's declared enum is silently dropped from the tool schema.

Concretely, for a command declared to match a hand-written schema that carries an enum:

```python
c = Command(path=("x",), tool="ddflow_x",
            params=(Param("mode", choices=("a", "b"), schema_enum=True),))
```

`Param("mode", choices=("a","b"), schema_enum=True).schema()` returns `{"type":"string","description":"","enum":["a","b"]}`, but `c.input_schema()` returns `{"type":"object","properties":{"mode":{"type":"string","description":""},"as_agent":{...}},"additionalProperties":False}` — no `enum`. So a command migrated with `schema_enum=True` to reproduce an existing `tools/list` schema produces different bytes than the hand-written one it is supposed to match (the exact parity the module exists to prove), and MCP clients no longer see the allowed values. The `schema_enum` field is effectively dead for every command that generates its schema through `Command`; only a direct `Param.schema()` call can ever emit an enum.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py — `Command.input_schema` / `Command.properties`

chunk_findings.detail: `Command.tier` is declared and documented as "the MCP tool tier", but `tool_entry()` (the method whose docstring says it returns "the entry the MCP engine's `TOOLS` table holds for this command") never writes a `"tier"` key: it emits only `description`, `properties`, `api`, `payload` and, conditionally, `text`/`kind`/`identify`/`deprecated`. `tier` appears nowhere else in the module (`input_schema`, `tool_listing`, `add_commands` do not read it), so it is write-only/dead. Concretely, `Command(path=("admin","wipe"), tool="ddflow_admin_wipe", tier="admin", call=...)` produces a `tool_entry()` identical to an entry declared `tier="standard"`; the engine, which dispatches off the `TOOLS` entry, therefore sees a default/standard tool (or, if it indexes `entry["tier"]`, gets a `KeyError`). Any command whose tier is not the default silently loses it, because the parity test only pins argparse help and the `tools/list` schema, not the dispatch entry's tier.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py — `Command.tool_entry`

chunk_findings.detail: For a positional parameter, `add_to` puts the bare name into `args` and never passes `required`, which is correct for argparse (positionals are mandatory without `nargs`/`default`), but the MCP side uses `self.required`, whose default is `False`. So `Param("file", positional=True)` (required left at the default) yields a schema where `"file"` is omitted from `required` — `params_schema` only lists `[p.name for p in shown if p.required]` — while `argparse` rejects an invocation that omits `file` with "the following arguments are required: file". The two surfaces generated from the one declaration disagree on whether the argument is required, and nothing in `__post_init__` forces `required=True` when `positional=True` to keep them in sync (unlike `repeat`, which is normalized to `type="array"`).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py — `Param.add_to` / `Param.spec`

chunk_findings.detail: `tool_entry()` is documented as "the entry the MCP engine's `TOOLS` table holds", but it never emits the `tier` field that `Command` declares for exactly that purpose ("``tier`` is the MCP tool tier"). Given `Command(path=("gate", "record"), tool="ddflow_gate_record", tier="advanced")`, the generated entry is `{"description": ..., "properties": ..., "api": ..., "payload": ...}` with no `"tier"` key, so an engine that groups/filters tools by tier (e.g. to keep `advanced` tools out of the default `tools/list`) will treat this command as the default `standard`. The same omission drops `render` (the declared "optional human renderer"), which likewise cannot reach the engine through this entry. The golden test described in the module docstring only compares argparse help and the `tools/list` schema, so neither omission can be caught by it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py `Command.tool_entry`

chunk_findings.detail: `params_schema()` advertises `"additionalProperties": False` while simultaneously removing every deprecated parameter from `properties` and `required`. So for a command declaring `deprecated={"old_arg": ...}`, the docstring's promise that the argument is "still ACCEPTED (D-compat) but is not advertised" and the emitted schema contradict each other: a client that validates its arguments against the served `inputSchema` (which now says unknown properties are forbidden) rejects `old_arg` before the request reaches the server that would still accept it — precisely the legacy callers the deprecation path exists to keep working. If deprecated args must remain usable through schema-validating clients, `additionalProperties: False` must not be emitted whenever `deprecated` is non-empty.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py `params_schema`

chunk_findings.detail: For a positional parameter, `add_to` puts the bare name into `args` and never passes `required`, which is correct for argparse (positionals are mandatory without `nargs`/`default`), but the MCP side uses `self.required`, whose default is `False`. The two surfaces generated from the one declaration disagree on whether the argument is required, and nothing in `__post_init__` forces `required=True` when `positional=True` to keep them in sync (unlike `repeat`, which is normalized to `type="array"`).
