chunk_findings.detail:
The entry claims two mutually exclusive things about the same command. `via=("ddflow_list",
"search")` declares that `ddflow_list` with the argument value `search` serves the CLI `search`
command, i.e. that such an MCP argument value exists and works today; the `reason` on that very
same `Command` says the opposite: "the consolidated MCP read tool that will carry it is the later
task B-view-mcp-list …, until then agents use `ddflow_recall` and `ddflow_history`". Since
`ROUTED_PATHS = routed_paths(EXEMPTIONS)` is derived from `via`, the parity test's routed/alias
table will contain `("search",) -> ("ddflow_list", "search")`. Whatever the test does with that
table, one of the two fields is wrong: if the test asserts the routed target exists, it fails for
every run (`ddflow_list` has no `search` source yet); if it merely exempts the path, `search` is
silently recorded as covered by a tool that the declaration itself says does not carry it, which
removes exactly the gap this table exists to keep visible. Compare the sibling viewers
(`task`/`phase`/`bug`/`lesson`/`session` `list`), for which `via` is asserted without any
"later task" caveat, showing that `via` is meant to denote present coverage.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/exemptions.py — `Command(path=("search",), via=("ddflow_list", "search"), reason=...)`

chunk_findings.detail:
The docstring states the parity test "used to hold these as five dicts (`NOT_EXPOSED`, `ALIASES`,
`LEAF_NOT_EXPOSED`, `LEAF_VIA`, `FLAG_EXEMPTIONS`, `PROSE_TOOLS`)" but lists six names, and the
derived names below the tuple are also six (`EXEMPT_PATHS`, `ROUTED_PATHS`, `COVERING_TOOLS`,
`EXEMPT_WORDS`, `FLAG_EXEMPT`, `PROSE_REASONS`). Anyone reconciling the migrated tables against
the old file will look for a fifth/sixth mismatch that does not exist; the count is simply wrong.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/exemptions.py — module docstring table count

chunk_findings.detail: `exempt_paths` only treats a command as "served, not exempt" when `len(c.via) == MAX_VIA`, i.e. only for the selector form `("tool", "selector")`. A one-element `via` (documented as "a one-element form names a tool that covers it whole (`init` -> `("ddflow_setup",)`)" and returned by `covering_tools`) is *also* a command that is served and has no tool of its own, so by the field's own definition it will typically carry a `reason` (the renamed docstring is "Why this command HAS NO MCP TOOL OF ITS OWN"). Concretely, a declaration `Command(path=("init",), via=("ddflow_setup",), reason="served by ddflow_setup")` makes `exempt_paths` return `{("init",): "served by ddflow_setup"}`, while `covering_tools` simultaneously returns `{"init": ("ddflow_setup",)}`. Since the derivation replaces the former hand-written tables (where `init` lived in the *via* table and not in the *not exposed* table), `init` now also appears in the derived "not exposed" set, which is wrong: it is served, not exempt. The docstring's own wording ("A command routed by a selector is served, not exempt, even when it also carries a reason") shows the intent is to exclude served commands, but the guard covers only the two-element case; it should exclude any non-empty `via` (e.g. `not c.via`) rather than `len(c.via) != MAX_VIA`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py: `exempt_paths`

chunk_findings.detail: The stated intent of this change is that the four MCP-parity exemption tables — *not exposed*, *via*, *flag* and *prose* — are being moved into `Command` fields, and the test is meant to derive its invariants from those fields. The new invariant in this diff is written as `if c.path and not (c.reason or c.via): raise AssertionError(f"{c.path}: a declaration with neither a reason nor a route")`, i.e. it only accepts `reason` or `via` as an acceptable declaration. But the same change introduces `flag` (and `prose`) as first-class exemption mechanisms — a command can be exempted from MCP parity because it is reachable via a flag, without being reachable via another command and without a prose/reason justification. For such a declaration, e.g. an `EXEMPTIONS` entry with `path=("scan",)`, `flag="--json"`, `reason=None`, `via=None`, both branches pass the reason-length guard (because `c.reason` is falsy) and then hit `c.path and not (None or None)` → the test raises `AssertionError: ('scan',): a declaration with neither a reason nor a route`, even though the declaration is valid under the model this change is building. The check's own message says "reason nor a route", yet it omits `flag` (and `prose`) from the set of routes, so any flag-only or prose-only exemption that lacks a `via`/`reason` will now produce a spurious test failure. The condition should include the other route fields (e.g. `not (c.reason or c.via or c.flag or c.prose)`).

chunk_findings.detail: `exempt_paths` filters with `len(c.via) != MAX_VIA`, so it excludes only the selector-routed form (`via` of length 2) and keeps any command that is covered whole by another tool (`via` of length 1) as long as it also has a `reason`. The docstring's own rule — a command "served" by another tool is "not exempt" — applies equally to the whole-cover form: a `via` of one ages `("ddflow_setup",)` explicitly means the command has no tool of its own but is still reachable. Concretely, given `Command(path=("init",), via=("ddflow_setup",), reason="...")`, `exempt_paths` returns `{("init",): "..."}`, i.e. `init` is published in the derived "not exposed" table even though it is actually exposed through `ddflow_setup`. The parity test that derives its tables from this function will therefore stop checking that `init` remains reachable via `ddflow_setup`, so a regression that drops `init` from that tool would not be caught — the exact class of gap the parity table exists to prevent. The guard should exclude any command that has a `via` at all (`not c.via`), not just the two-element one.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py `exempt_paths` (new function, ~line 296)

chunk_findings.detail: The migrated `EXEMPT_WORDS` is not the old `NOT_EXPOSED`: it is derived from every exemption `Command` that carries a `reason`, *including* commands that also carry a `via` route. The change's own fixture proves this. `test_exemption_derivations` declares `Command(path=("init",), reason="r"*30, via=("ddflow_setup",))` and asserts `R.declared_words(cmds) == {"mcp", "init", "search"}`, i.e. the aliased command `init` (and the routed command `search`, `reason` + `via=("ddflow_list","search")`) end up in `EXEMPT_WORDS`, even though `init` is also in `coveral_tools`/`COVERING_TOOLS`. Because `covered()` now short-circuits at `if cmd in EXEMPT_WORDS: return True`, the alias branch (`for alias in ALIASES.get(cmd, ()): if alias in TOOLS`) is dead for any exemption declared with both a `reason` and a `via`. Concrete failure: keep the (supported, tested) shape `Command(path=("init",), reason=..., via=("ddflow_setup",))` in `surfaces/exemptions.py` and delete `ddflow_setup` from `ddflow.surfaces.mcp.TOOLS`. Before this diff, `"init"` lived only in `ALIASES`, so `covered("init")` was `False` once the alias target disappeared and the parity test failed; after this diff `covered("init")` returns `True` on the `reason` alone, so the command is accepted as "covered" although it is now neither exposed nor routed to any tool. The same masking applies to `search` (`reason` + `via=("ddflow_list","search")`): `covered("search")` no longer depends on `ddflow_list` being present in `TOOLS`. The parity table thus silently broadens compared with the old disjoint `NOT_EXPOSED`/`ALIASES` pair.

chunk_findings.detail:
`exempt_paths` only withholds a command from the exemption table when `len(c.via) == MAX_VIA` (the selector form), so a command carrying the *one-element* covered form plus a `reason` is emitted into `EXEMPT_PATHS` even though it is served and has no exemption of its own. Concrete input: `Command(path=("init",), via=("ddflow_setup",), reason="covered by ddflow_setup")` (exactly the shape the new `via` field docstring advertises: "a one-element form names a tool that covers it whole (`init` -> `("ddflow_setup",)`)"). This command has no MCP tool of its own, so by the `reason` field's own definition ("Why this command has no MCP tool of its own") it legitimately carries a `reason`, and the well-formedness rule the change adds elsewhere is an OR — `not (c.reason or c.via)` — which explicitly permits `reason` and `via` to co-occur. The result is that `exempt_paths` returns `{("init",): "..."} ...` while `covering_tools` simultaneously returns `{"init": ("ddflow_setup",)}`: the same command is declared both "exempt (no tool)" and "covered whole by a tool", and `EXEMPT_PATHS` (the migration of `NOT_EXPOSED`) gains one-word entries that were never exemptions.

The earlier triage of this issue ("refuted") does not answer it: its probe states that old `LEAF_NOT_EXPOSED` held `init`/`adopt`/`config` with a one-element via and that "the derived table equals it". But the only derived table keyed by word is `declared_words`, which requires `not c.via`; a command with a one-element via can therefore never appear in `declared_words`, so the asserted equality is impossible for exactly those entries and the probe says nothing about whether they leak into `exempt_paths`. (The same over-permissiveness also catches any two-word command served whole by a one-element via, since `covering_tools` further requires `len(c.path) == 1`.)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py:exempt_paths (and the `len(c.via) != MAX_VIA` filter)

chunk_findings.detail: The reworked test no longer validates every exemption it used to. The staleness list is now built from `EXEMPT_WORDS`, whereas the old test built it from `NOT_EXPOSED` — the table of exempt *command paths*. In this rework the derived table for exempt path declarations is `EXEMPT_PATHS` (the successor of `NOT_EXPOSED`, whose entries are the same `Command`s iterated by the new reason loop), while `EXEMPT_WORDS` is the table of the leaf/via selector words. As a result, a command exemption declared as a path (e.g. a `Command(path=("config","set"), ...)` carried in `EXEMPT_PATHS`/`EXEMPTIONS`) is no longer checked: if `config set` is removed from the CLI, `stale` stays empty and `assert not stale` passes, so a dangling exemption for a command that no longer exists survives the "only shrinks" guard. The second check is narrowed the same way by `if len(c.path) == 1 and c.reason:`: entries whose path has more than one element are excluded from the `len(reason) > 20` check entirely, so such an entry can carry a stub reason (`reason="todo"`) and still pass, even though the previous `for cmd, reason in NOT_EXPOSED.items(): assert len(reason) > 20` required a real reason for every entry. Both invariants need to be applied to the union of exempt declarations (`EXEMPTIONS`, or `EXEMPT_WORDS` plus `EXEMPT_PATHS`), not to `EXEMPT_WORDS` / single-element paths alone.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_parity.py:test_the_exemption_list_only_shrinks

chunk_findings.detail: These commands are each declared with a `reason` that says another tool serves them — e.g. `Command(path=("hooks","status"), reason="covered by ddflow_hooks, whose action argument selects it")`, `Command(path=("prompts","show"), reason="covered by ddflow_prompts, whose action argument selects it")`, `Command(path=("companions","list"), reason="covered by ddflow_companions")`, `Command(path=("reviewers","detect"), reason="covered by ddflow_reviewers_detect")` — but none of them carry the `via` field that the module docstring defines as "the tool, and the argument value, that serves it". Compare the sibling routed entries, which encode exactly the same relationship machine-readably: `Command(path=("task","list"), via=("ddflow_list","task"))`, `Command(path=("phase","list"), via=("ddflow_list","phase"))`, and the whole-cover aliases `Command(path=("config",), reason=..., via=("ddflow_configure",))`, `Command(path=("init",), reason=..., via=("ddflow_setup",))`. Because `via` is empty, `routed_paths(EXEMPTIONS)`/`ROUTED_PATHS` (the migrated `LEAF_VIA` table) contains `("task","list") -> ddflow_list` but not `("hooks","status") -> ddflow_hooks`, and `exempt_paths` files the latter as a plain "no tool of its own" exemption rather than a routed one. Concretely, given `EXEMPTIONS` as written, `ROUTED_PATHS` silently loses the hooks/prompts/companions/reviewers routes that the old `LEAF_VIA` held, so `test_mcp_parity` can no longer verify that `ddflow_hooks`, `ddflow_prompts` and `ddflow_companions` actually expose an `action`/view value for each of `status`, `install`, `uninstall`, `list`, `show`, `eject`, `get` — a command could drop its MCP coverage with the parity test still green. These entries need `via=("ddflow_hooks","status")` (etc.) for the selector-selected family, and `via=("ddflow_reviewers_detect",)` / `via=("ddflow_companions_add",)` / `via=("ddflow_recall",)` for the whole-tool covers, matching the `ddflow_list`/`ddflow_setup`/`ddflow_configure` entries.

chunk_findings.detail: These commands are each declared with a `reason` that says another tool serves them — e.g. `Command(path=("hooks","status"), reason="covered by ddflow_hooks, whose action argument selects it")`, `Command(path=("prompts","show"), reason="covered by ddflow_prompts, whose action argument selects it")`, `Command(path=("companions","list"), reason="covered by ddflow_companions")`, `Command(path=("reviewers","detect"), reason="covered by ddflow_reviewers_detect")` — but none of them carry the `via` field that the module docstring defines as "the tool, and the argument value, that serves it". Compare the sibling routed entries, which encode exactly the same relationship machine-readably: `Command(path=("task","list"), via=("ddflow_list","task"))`, `Command(path=("phase","list"), via=("ddflow_list","phase"))`, and the whole-cover aliases `Command(path=("config",), reason=..., via=("ddflow_configure",))`, `Command(path=("init",), reason=..., via=("ddflow_setup",))`. chunk_findings.detail: The collision guard added in `register()` only checks the alias side of the rename: for each `old` in the current knob's `renamed_from`, it raises if `old` is already a live key (`old in DECLARED`). It never checks the reverse direction — when a field whose `key` is itself already registered in `RENAMED` is declared as a live knob. Because fields are processed in declaration order and resolution is a single pass, the guard fires only if the *live* key is declared before the alias, not after. Concretely, given section modules registered in the order (A then B): A's class has a knob `b.x` with `renamed_from=("b.y",)`, so during A's registration `RENAMED["b.y"] = ("b.x", ...)`. Then B declares the live knob `b.y`; when its field is processed, `DECLARED["b.y"]` is set, but the `for old in meta.renamed_from:` loop only inspects `b.y`'s own (empty) `renamed_from`, so nothing raises, and the registry now contains both `DECLARED["b.y"]` (a live key) and `RENAMED["b.y"]` (an alias for `b.x`). The exact conflict the guard was written to prevent ("X is renamed_from of Y but is also a live key") is silently accepted whenever the live key is registered after its alias. Reversing the two module imports changes the outcome, so the guard's behavior depends on section registration order, which is import-order, not on any property of the declarations themselves.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/_docs.py (register loop, `old in DECLARED` guard)

chunk_findings.detail:
The emptiness probe uses the full dotted section name against a `tomllib` result, which nests tables: `tomllib.loads(text).get(osec, {"x": 1})` for `osec = "gate.unit_tests"` never finds the key (`tomllib` gives `{"gate": {"unit_tests": {...}}}`, and `.get("gate.unit_tests")` returns the truthy `{"x": 1}` sentinel), so the `not ...` clause is always `False` and the emptied old table is never dropped. Concrete input: `RENAMED` maps `gate.unit_tests.command -> gate.commands.unit`; the file contains
```
[gate.unit_tests]
command = "pytest"
```
After any write, the key moves to `[gate.commands]` but the now-empty `[gate.unit_tests]` table remains, contradicting the function's contract ("An old table left empty is dropped too unless it is one of the `live` section names"). The follow-on line `del doc[osec]` is consistent with that misunderstanding: it indexes the tomlkit document with the whole dotted string as a single key, so if the guard ever did turn `True` for a dotted `osec` it would raise `KeyError` (tomlkit requires `del doc["gate"]["unit_tests"]`, not `del doc["gate.unit_tests"]`), and in the contrived case where a top-level quoted key literally named `"gate.unit_tests"` coexists with the nested table it would delete that unrelated key instead of the nested table.

(The rest of the hunk — moving the old value, preferring an already-present new spelling, top-level-key asymmetry — either matches the stated contract or is unreachable for this project's key shapes.)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/tomlcfg.py:263 (`move_keys` empty-table drop)

chunk_findings.detail: The regex `invalid choice: '([^']*)'` fires for *every* argparse "invalid choice" error, but the code then builds the suggestion exclusively from the parser's **subcommand** names (`for a in self._actions if isinstance(a, argparse._SubParsersAction)`). Choice-constrained options and positionals produce the identical message shape, so a mistyped option value gets a bogus "Did you mean '<command>'?". Example: a parser with subcommands `search`, `serve` and an option `--mode choices=["table","json"]`; running `--mode sear` yields `argument --mode: invalid choice: 'sear' (choose from 'table', 'json') Did you mean 'search'?` — the suggestion points at an unrelated command and actively misdirects the user. The override should verify that the failing action is a `_SubParsersAction` before appending a command suggestion.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py — `SuggestingParser.error`

chunk_findings.detail: `used_aliases` walks the ancestor chain to collect deprecated *command* aliases (`node = sub.choices[typed]` per level), but for *flag* aliases it consults only the final parser: `flags = getattr(node, "_compat_flags", {})`. A deprecated flag alias declared on an ancestor parser is therefore never reported. Concretely, if a global flag `--color` carries the alias `--colour` registered on the root parser, `ddflow search --colour` ends with `node` = the `search` parser, whose `_compat_flags` does not contain `--colour`, so the one-line notice required by D-compat is silently skipped even though the alias was used. The lookup needs to merge `_compat_flags` along the walked chain (or the root parser's table) rather than only the leaf.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py — `used_aliases`

chunk_findings.detail:
`Command.__post_init__` still validates only the canonical parameter names (`names = [p.name for p in self.params]`), while the new alias machinery introduces additional argument names that live in the same MCP namespace. `_check_aliases` is invoked per-parameter with a single canonical name (`Param.__post_init__` passes only `self.name`), so nothing ever checks an alias against *another* parameter's name or against another parameter's alias.

Concretely, a command defined as

```python
Command(
    path=("show",),
    params=[
        Param(name="source", type="string", ...),                 # canonical MCP arg / CLI --source
        Param(name="sources", aliases=("source",), deprecated_since="0.9", type="string", ...),
    ],
)
```

passes `__post_init__`: the canonical list is `["source", "sources"]`, no duplicates. But `Param(name="sources").arg_aliases()` returns `{"source": Alias(...)}`, so the MCP surface now has two parameters claiming the argument name `source` — either the alias silently shadows the real `source` argument (wrong value routed) or the alias is unreachable (violating "always callable"); whichever the (unseen) dispatcher does, the registry has accepted an ambiguous definition it should have rejected. Note the asymmetry this creates: on the CLI the same definition *is* rejected, but only later, in `Param`'s parser-registration method, because the alias `source` becomes `--source` and the guard `if option in parser._option_string_actions: raise ValueError(...)` fires. For an MCP-only command (`path=()`, no CLI parser is ever built) the collision is never detected at all, so the bad definition survives into `tools/list` and MCP dispatch.

A corresponding check (alias vs. every other param's name and vs. every other param's aliases) is missing from `Command.__post_init__`/`_check_aliases`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py: Command.__post_init__ (alias uniqueness)

chunk_findings.detail:
Both new `Alias` constructions pass the removal version as the *fifth positional* argument:

- `Alias("tool", a, self.tool, self.deprecated_since, self.removed_in)` (`tool_alias_list`)
- `Alias("command", old, " ".join(self.path), self.deprecated_since, self.removed_in)` (`add_to`)

The alias record carries the three deprecation fields in the order stated by this change's own metadata — `deprecated_since`, `replacement`, `removed_in` (the new spec/Command/Param fields are `aliases`, `deprecated_since`, `replacement`, `removed_in`). Passing `self.removed_in` positionally therefore binds it to `replacement` and leaves `removed_in` at its default. Concretely, an alias declared with `removed_in="1.0"` (e.g. the `doc`→`docs` group alias or `rules`→`rule`) yields an `Alias` whose `removed_in` is unset — so the "removed_in must be >= 1.0" enforcement and any "will be removed in X" notice are wrong/bypassed — while `replacement` is populated with a bare version string, so the one-line notice/compat metadata for every alias is incorrect. The call sites should use the keyword (`removed_in=self.removed_in`) or pass `replacement` explicitly.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py — `Command.tool_alias_list` and `Command.add_to`

chunk_findings.detail: The test's stated property is that the CLI alias notice is printed once per session, but the deduplication is never exercised. It calls `cli.main(["display", "I1"])` exactly once and then calls `cli.main(["show", "I1"])`, i.e. the second invocation does not use the alias at all, so no notice would ever be emitted from it even if dedup were entirely absent. Concretely, an implementation that re-prints "'display' is deprecated ..." on *every* alias use would still pass: `ran == ["I1"]`, `err.count("deprecated") == 1` (first call), and the second `readouterr().err` is empty. This is aggravated by the monkeypatch `cli.build_parser = lambda: _parser(cmd)`, which builds a fresh parser per `main()` call: if the `Notices` state is carried on the parser (which `used_aliases(root, ...)` and `R.Notices()` suggest is the design) rather than module-globally, running `ddflow display I1` twice in one process would print the notice twice, and this test would still pass. To catch the bug the test would need a second `cli.main(["display", "I1"])` (or equivalent) call and to assert the notice is not repeated; the MCP (`test_the_tool_notice_is_said_once_per_session`), argument (`test_an_old_argument_works_is_hidden_and_notices_once`) and config (`test_an_old_config_key_is_read_with_one_warning`) tests all do perform the repeat-with-the-old-name call, making this CLI test the only "once" test that is vacuous.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_compat_aliases.py::test_main_says_so_once_on_stderr

chunk_findings.detail:
The conflict check is one-directional and evaluated only at the moment a `renamed_from` carrier is registered, so a *live* key that is registered later silently coexists with an alias of the same name. `DECLARED[key] = meta` is assigned for the current knob before the loop, and the loop only asks `old in DECLARED`; nothing prevents a subsequent knob from taking a key that already lives in `RENAMED`. Two concrete triggers:

- Same class, field order dependent: declare `foo = knob(..., renamed_from=("docs.other",))` before another knob `other` in the same section. When `foo` is processed, `DECLARED` does not yet contain `"docs.other"`, so no `ValueError` is raised; then `"docs.other"` is registered as a live knob. Now `"docs.other"` is both a live key and an entry in `RENAMED["docs.other"] = ("docs.foo", ...)`, so the alias-resolution path (which reads `RENAMED` to warn + migrate the old key) will shadow the genuinely live knob. Swapping the two field declarations makes the exact same configuration raise `ValueError`. 
- Cross-module: if the section that owns the alias is imported before the section that declares the colliding live key, registration succeeds with an ambiguous key; importing them in the other order raises. Behaviour therefore depends on import/declaration order rather than on the configuration itself.

The register hook needs to reject a live `key` that is already present in `RENAMED` (e.g. `if key in RENAMED: raise ...`) in addition to the existing alias-side check, so a `renamed_from` old name can never also be a live key regardless of declaration/import order.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/_docs.py:register (the `renamed_from` loop)

chunk_findings.detail: `osec` is produced by `old.rpartition(".")`, so for any renamed knob whose dotted path has more than one component before the last dot — exactly the shape used as the running example in this file, e.g. `gate.unit_tests.command`, where `osec == "gate.unit_tests"` — the emptiness test asks `tomllib.loads(text).get("gate.unit_tests", {"x": 1})`. Since `tomllib` parses that text into `{"gate": {"unit_tests": {...}}}`, the top-level lookup never finds the key and always falls back to the truthy default `{"x": 1}`; `not <truthy>` is `False`, so the branch is never taken and the emptied parent table is never removed, contradicting the documented contract ("An old table left empty is dropped too unless it is one of the `live` section names"). Concretely, with `RENAMED` containing `gate.unit_tests.rules -> gate.unit_tests.rule` and a config file whose `[gate.unit_tests]` table contains only `rules = 1`, `move_keys` removes the key and then writes `rule = 1` back, leaving a stale `[gate.unit_tests]` shell behind (the `del doc[osec]` that is supposed to clean it up is unreachable for this shape, and would in fact raise `KeyError`/delete the wrong thing if the check were ever satisfied, because `osec` is a dotted path rather than a top-level key). Either the lookup must navigate `osec` the same way the value-side lookup navigates `nsec`, or the parent path must be split off before the `del`.
chunk_findings.location: ddflow/infra/tomlcfg.py `move_keys` (the empty-table check `not tomllib.loads(text).get(osec, {"x": 1})` paired with `del doc[osec]`)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/tomlcfg.py `move_keys` (the empty-table check `not tomllib.loads(text).get(osec, {"x": 1})` paired with `del doc[osec]`)

chunk_findings.detail: The command loop descends to the deepest command parser and then collects flag aliases only from that final `node` (`flags = getattr(node, "_compat_flags", {})`). Flag aliases declared on any ancestor parser — including the root parser, where global options live — are never consulted, so their notice is never produced. Concrete input: a global option registered on the root parses as `Alias(kind="flag", old="--old-verbose", new="--verbose", ...)`, with root `_compat_flags["--old-verbose"] = that alias`. Running `ddflow --old-verbose docs` parses fine (the alias is a real argument on the root parser), but `used_aliases(root, args, ["--old-verbose", "docs"])` sets `node` to the `docs` parser and reads `docs._compat_flags` (empty), returning `[]`; the required one-line deprecation notice is silently skipped. The same happens for `ddflow config --old-flag set` when the flag is declared on the intermediate `config` parser. To satisfy the function's own contract ("the flags typed"), `_compat_flags` must be gathered from every parser visited along the chain, not just the leaf.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py:used_aliases

chunk_findings.detail: The handler triggers on `re.search(r"invalid choice: '([^']*)'", message)`, which matches the `invalid choice` text produced by `_check_value` for *any* argument with `choices`, not just the subparsers action. It then appends a command suggestion drawn from the subparser choices. Concrete input: on a root parser with subcommands (e.g. a command named `list`) and an option `--level` with `choices=["low","high"]`, running `ddflow --level lisp` yields the error `argument --level: invalid choice: 'lisp' (choose from 'low', 'high')`, and `error()` appends ` Did you mean 'list'?` — suggesting a command name as a correction for an option value, which cannot be a valid value of `--level`. The suggestion should be limited to the message generated for the subparsers action (e.g. by checking the action/`argument <name>:` prefix or by only handling `_SubParsersAction` errors).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py:SuggestingParser.error

chunk_findings.detail: A `Param` declared as positional can legally carry a `-`-prefixed alias, yet that alias is registered on no surface at all. `_check_aliases(f"param {self.name!r}", self.aliases, self.name, ...)` is only handed the alias tuple, the canonical *name* and the deprecation fields — it is never told the param is positional and (per the field's own docstring) must accept `-`-prefixed spellings as CLI-only flag spellings. So for e.g. `Param(name="file", positional=True, aliases=("-f",), deprecated_since="0.5")` validation passes, but `arg_aliases()` drops it (`if not a.startswith("-")`) and `flag_aliases()` short-circuits to `{}` for positionals. The result is a configured alias that is silently uncallable — `-f` is not in the MCP argument alias map and not in the CLI option map — contradicting the stated guarantee that aliases are "always callable", with no construction-time error to tell the author the alias is dead. Either `__post_init__` must reject `-`-prefixed aliases on positionals, or `flag_aliases()`/`arg_aliases()` must surface them.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py — `Param.arg_aliases()` / `Param.flag_aliases()`

chunk_findings.detail: `unknown_arg_hint(known: Iterable[str], unknown: Iterable[str])` re-uses the `known` iterable once per unknown name (`pairs = [(u, closest(u, known)) for u in unknown]`). The annotation promises any `Iterable[str]`, but for a one-shot iterable (a generator, which is a perfectly valid `Iterable[str]`) the first `closest` call consumes it and every later call matches against an empty sequence. Concretely, `unknown_arg_hint((n for n in ("source", "format")), ["sorce", "fromat"])` returns ` Did you mean 'source' (for 'sorce')?` and silently drops the second suggestion, because `format` is no longer in the exhausted generator — so an MCP client that misspells more than one argument only gets a hint for the first. Materialising `known` (e.g. `known = list(known)`) once before the comprehension fixes it. Severity is low because it only misfires when a caller passes a non-re-iterable; with a list/set it behaves as intended.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py `unknown_arg_hint`

chunk_findings.detail:
The emptiness probe passes the full dotted section name to a single top-level `dict.get`. `tomllib.loads` returns nested tables, so for any `osec` that itself contains a dot (e.g. `osec == "gate.unit_tests"` for the key `gate.unit_tests.command`), `tomllib.loads(text).get(osec)` never finds the table and falls back to the truthy sentinel `{"x": 1}`, making `not ...` always `False`; the emptied old table is therefore never dropped, contradicting the function's own docstring ("An old table left empty is dropped too unless it is one of the ``live`` section names"). Concrete input: old = `gate.unit_tests.command`, file is `[gate.unit_tests]\ncommand = "x"\n`; after the move the file keeps a dangling empty `[gate.unit_tests]` header.

This is the finding the previous review reported and triaged as refuted, and I am re-reporting it because the refuting probe does not answer it: `knob(renamed_from=('gate.unit_tests.command',)) raising "not a 'section.knob' key"` only constrains the *knob metadata* helper to single-dot keys; it says nothing about `RENAMED`, the config rename map `move_keys` is actually fed here, whose keys are config-file paths. That nested section names are in scope for this function is shown by (a) this diff's own caller example, `"gate.unit_tests.command"`, used as the canonical illustration of a valid `<section>.<key>`, and (b) `move_keys` itself splitting `osec`/`nsec` on `"."` to navigate nested tables. Any entry of the form `gate.unit_tests.*` (or any other multi-segment section) in `RENAMED` therefore silently skips the drop step. (Note the probe bug is also the only thing preventing `del doc[osec]` from raising `KeyError` on such an `osec`, since tomlkit is indexed by the first path segment only — a proper fix must navigate to the real parent table rather than delete `doc[osec]` directly.)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/tomlcfg.py `move_keys` (emptiness probe, `tomllib.loads(text).get(osec, {"x": 1})`)

chunk_findings.detail: The deprecation-alias bookkeeping is stored in a module-global `Notices` instance, so "one notice per session" is implemented as "one notice per Python process". `main()` is a plain function taking `argv` and is invoked more than once in a single process by design (the project's own tests call `cli.main([...])` repeatedly; any wrapper/embedder may do the same). Each such call is a distinct CLI invocation, i.e. a distinct session, yet it shares the already-populated `_NOTICES`. Concretely, `cli.main(["display", "I1"])` followed by `cli.main(["display", "I1"])` prints the `'display' is deprecated` line only for the first call — the second invocation silently drops the notice even though it is a fresh session — and if any earlier `main()` call anywhere in the process already used `display`, the notice never appears at all. Because there is no reset hook, the behavior is order-dependent across tests/invocations, so the "notices once" property can neither be isolated nor relied upon. The inline comment ("one CLI process is one session") only holds for the production entry point, which calls `main` exactly once; it does not hold for the in-process callers the tests actually use.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/cli.py:321 (`_NOTICES = Notices()`)

chunk_findings.detail: The `Alias`'s replacement/`new` slot for a *flag* alias is built as `self.replacement or self.option`. `self.option` is a CLI spelling (`--source`), but `self.replacement` is the same raw string that `arg_aliases` uses as an MCP *argument* name. Those two conventions are incompatible, so one of the flag cases is necessarily wrong. Concretely, for `Param(name="source", aliases=("src",), replacement="datasource")`, `flag_aliases()` yields `--src -> Alias("flag", "--src", "datasource", ...)`, i.e. the flag's replacement has no `--`; the CLI deprecation notice/suggestion for `--src` will therefore tell the user to use `"datasource"` rather than an option string. For the same param with `replacement` unset, `flag_aliases()` yields `new == "--source"` (dashed), so a consumer that prints `Alias.new` verbatim is wrong in exactly one of the two cases, and a consumer that dashes it itself is wrong in the other. There is no value a developer can put in `replacement` that is simultaneously a valid bare MCP argument name (as `arg_aliases` requires) and a valid CLI option spelling (as `flag_aliases`'s default `self.option` uses).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py — `Param.flag_aliases` (the `self.replacement or self.option` third argument)

chunk_findings.detail: The loop that turns `group_aliases` into callable top-level names validates only that the *target* group exists (`if group not in made: raise ValueError(...)`); it never validates `alias.old` itself. `add_command_alias` is handed the top-level `subparsers` action, and argparse resolves a subparser by indexing that action's flat `_name_parser_map`, so the alias name is written into the same namespace that already holds the live group names. The other direction of the same collision class *was* guarded elsewhere (finding 1, the knob-rename guard), and parameter aliases were given an explicit uniqueness check (finding 5), but this path has neither. Concrete input: a registry that declares commands under groups `search` and `serve`, plus `group_aliases={"serve": [Alias(old="search", ...)]}`. The earlier command loop has already inserted `parsers["search"]` into the root name map; the group-alias loop then overwrites that entry with the `serve` parser, so `ddflow search --source ...` silently dispatches into the `serve` group instead of `search`, with no error at declaration or call time. The same works in reverse if a live key is declared after its old name, exactly the ordering hole described in finding 1, now in the parser registry rather than the config registry.
chunk_findings.location: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py (group alias registration loop, `add_command_alias(subparsers, parsers[group], alias.old, alias)`)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py (group alias registration loop, `add_command_alias(subparsers, parsers[group], alias.old, alias)`)

chunk_findings.detail: This test is presented as the probe for the confirmed finding that `SuggestingParser.error` builds a bogus command suggestion for *any* `invalid choice:` message. But it parses `["search", "--mode", "sear"]`, where `--mode` is a parameter of the `search` command, so the error is raised by the `search` parser. That parser is a leaf: `self._actions` contains no `argparse._SubParsersAction`, so the reported buggy implementation (`for a in self._actions if isinstance(a, argparse._SubParsersAction)`) collects no candidate names and emits no suggestion either way. The test therefore passes with and without the fix and does not pin it. The scenario the finding actually describes — a parser that *itself* has subcommands **and** a choice-constrained option (e.g. the root/group parser with `--mode choices=["table","json"]`), where `error()` runs on a parser whose `_actions` does contain a `_SubParsersAction` and would still produce `Did you mean '<command>'?` for a mistyped option value — is not covered anywhere in the file. A correct probe would have to raise the choice error on a parser that also owns subparsers (or otherwise assert that the offending action is the subparsers action), which this test never does.

chunk_findings.detail:
The loop reuses one error message for three distinct conflict conditions:

```python
for old in meta.renamed_from:
    if old == key or old in RENAMED or old in DECLARED:
        raise ValueError(f"{old} is renamed_from of {key} but is also a live key")
    RENAMED[old] = (key, meta.since, meta.removed_in)
```

For the `old in RENAMED` arm the claim "but is also a live key" is false: a name can only be in `RENAMED` because it was registered as an alias of some *other* knob, never as a live key (any live declaration of that name would have been rejected earlier, and the `old in DECLARED` arm covers that separate case). Concrete input:

```python
class S:
    a = knob(1, renamed_from=("s.old",), since="0.9")
    b = knob(2, renamed_from=("s.old",), since="0.9")
```

Processing `a` sets `DECLARED["s.a"]` and `RENAMED["s.old"] = ("s.a", ...)`. `add_command_alias` guards only the direction it can see: `if word in table: raise` rejects a word that is already a command or alias *at the moment the alias is registered*. The plain dict key wins over `__missing__`, so the hidden alias entry becomes dead, while `subparsers._compat[word]` (set by `add_command_alias`) is never cleared. Two observable consequences:

1. The alias silently stops working (calling the alias runs the newly registered canonical command) — the "aliases are always callable" contract is broken with no error.

chunk_findings.detail: Registering a flag alias by putting it directly into `parser._option_string_actions` (without extending `action.option_strings`) makes the alias participate in argparse's prefix-abbreviation matching, because argparse's `_get_option_tuples` iterates `self._option_string_actions`, not `action.option_strings`. Concretely: the rename `doc -> docs` gives a `Param` for `docs` with `aliases=("doc",)`, hence canonical `--docs` and alias `--doc`, both pointing at the same action. A previously-valid abbreviated invocation `prog --do x` now hits `_parse_optional("--do")` -> `_get_option_tuples("--do")`, which returns two tuples (`--docs` and `--doc`), so argparse executes `self.error("ambiguous option: --do could match --docs, --doc")`. Before this change `--do` unambiguously resolved to `--docs`. Note the two matches belong to the *same* action, so even the action-vs-own-alias case is reported as ambiguous, and this affects every rename in the stated scope (`doc->docs`, `rules->rule`, etc.) for any caller that relied on argparse abbreviation (default `allow_abbrev=True`; the failure does not occur only if the parsers are constructed with `allow_abbrev=False`, which is not established anywhere I can see). So the compat layer turns a set of previously working command lines into hard errors.

chunk_findings.detail:
The emptiness probe passes the full dotted section name to a single top-level `dict.get`. `tomllib.loads` returns nested tables, so for any `osec` that itself contains a dot (e.g. `osec == "gate.unit_tests"` for the key `gate.unit_tests.command`), `tomllib.loads(text).get(osec)` never finds the table and falls back to the truthy sentinel `{"x": 1}`, making `not ...` always `False`; the emptied old table is therefore never dropped, contradicting the function's own docstring ("An old table left empty is dropped too unless it is one of the ``live`` section names"). Concrete input: old = `gate.unit_tests.command`, file is `[gate.unit_tests]\ncommand = "x"\n`; after the move the file keeps a dangling empty `[gate.unit_tests]` header.

This is the finding the previous review reported and triaged as refuted, and I am re-reporting it because the refuting probe does not answer it: `knob(renamed_from=('gate.unit_tests.command',)) raising "not a 'section.knob' key"` only constrains the *knob metadata* helper to single-dot keys; it says nothing about `RENAMED`, the config rename map `move_keys` is actually fed here, whose keys are config-file paths. That nested section names are in scope for this function is shown by (a) this diff's own caller example, `"gate.unit_tests.command"`, used as the canonical illustration of a valid `<section>.<key>`, and (b) `move_keys` itself splitting `osec`/`nsec` on `"."` to navigate nested tables. Any entry of the form `gate.unit_tests.*` (or any other multi-segment section) in `RENAMED` therefore silently skips the drop step. (Note the probe bug is also the only thing preventing `del doc[osec]` from raising `KeyError` on such an `osec`, since tomlkit is indexed by the first path segment only — a proper fix must navigate to the real parent table rather than delete `doc[osec]` directly.)

chunk_findings.detail: The deprecation-alias bookkeeping is stored in a module-global `Notices` instance, so "one notice per session" is implemented as "one notice per Python process". `main()` is a plain function taking `argv` and is invoked more than once in a single process by design (the project's own tests call `cli.main([...])` repeatedly; any wrapper/embedder may do the same). Each such call is a distinct CLI invocation, i.e. a distinct session, yet it shares the already-populated `_NOTICES`. Concretely, `cli.main(["display", "I1"])` followed by `cli.main(["display", "I1"])` prints the `'display' is deprecated` line only for the first call — the second invocation silently drops the notice even though it is a fresh session — and if any earlier `main()` call anywhere in the process already used `display`, the notice never appears at all. Because there is no reset hook, the behavior is order-dependent across tests/invocations, so the "notices once" property can neither be isolated nor relied upon. The inline comment ("one CLI process is one session") only holds for the production entry point, which calls `main` exactly once; it does not hold for the in-process callers the tests actually use.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/cli.py:321 (`_NOTICES = Notices()`)

chunk_findings.detail: The `Alias`'s replacement/`new` slot for a *flag* alias is built as `self.replacement or self.option`. `self.option` is a CLI spelling (`--source`), but `self.replacement` is the same raw string that `arg_aliases` uses as an MCP *argument* name. Those two conventions are incompatible, so one of the flag cases is necessarily wrong. Concretely, for `Param(name="source", aliases=("src",), replacement="datasource")`, `flag_aliases()` yields `--src -> Alias("flag", "--src", "datasource", ...)`, i.e. the flag's replacement has no `--`; the CLI deprecation notice/suggestion for `--src` will therefore tell the user to use `"datasource"` rather than an option string. For the same param with `replacement` unset, `flag_aliases()` yields `new == "--source"` (dashed), so a consumer that prints `Alias.new` verbatim is wrong in exactly one of the two cases, and a consumer that dashes it itself is wrong in the other. There is no value a developer can put in `replacement` that is simultaneously a valid bare MCP argument name (as `arg_aliases` requires) and a valid CLI option spelling (as `flag_aliases`'s default `self.option` uses).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py — `Param.flag_aliases` (the `self.replacement or self.option` third argument)

chunk_findings.detail: The loop that turns `group_aliases` into callable top-level names validates only that the *target* group exists (`if group not in made: raise ValueError(...)`); it never validates `alias.old` itself. `add_command_alias` is handed the top-level `subparsers` action, and argparse resolves a subparser by indexing that action's flat `_name_parser_map`, so the alias name is written into the same namespace that already holds the live group names. The other direction of the same collision class *was* guarded elsewhere (finding 1, the knob-rename guard), and parameter aliases were given an explicit uniqueness check (finding 5), but this path has neither. Concrete input: a registry that declares commands under groups `search` and `serve`, plus `group_aliases={"serve": [Alias(old="search", ...)]}`. The earlier command loop has already inserted `parsers["search"]` into the root name map; the group-alias loop then overwrites that entry with the `serve` parser, so `ddflow search --source ...` silently dispatches into the `serve` group instead of `search`, with no error at declaration or call time. The same works in reverse if a live key is declared after its old name, exactly the ordering hole described in finding 1, now in the parser registry rather than the config registry.

chunk_findings.detail: This test is presented as the probe for the confirmed finding that `SuggestingParser.error` builds a bogus command suggestion for *any* `invalid choice:` message. But it parses `["search", "--mode", "sear"]`, where `--mode` is a parameter of the `search` command, so the error is raised by the `search` parser. That parser is a leaf: `self._actions` contains no `argparse._SubParsersAction`, so the reported buggy implementation (`for a in self._actions if isinstance(a, argparse._SubParsersAction)`) collects no candidate names and emits no suggestion either way. The test therefore passes with and without the fix and does not pin it. The scenario the finding actually describes — a parser that *itself* has subcommands **and** a choice-constrained option (e.g. the root/group parser with `--mode choices=["table","json"]`), where `error()` runs on a parser whose `_actions` does contain a `_SubParsersAction` and would still produce `Did you mean '<command>'?` for a mistyped option value — is not covered anywhere in the file. A correct probe would have to raise the choice error on a parser that also owns subparsers (or otherwise assert that the offending action is the subparsers action), which this test never does.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_wrong_views` builds `paths` from *every* entry in `wrong` and then emits it as the set of files to rewrite and stage: " ddflow render" + _out_hint(paths), " git add " + " ".join(shlex.quote(p) for p in paths), but it also detects `newer` and appends the note "A view written at a newer format level is not regenerated by this ddflow: upgrade ddflow first." Those two statements are mutually exclusive for the same path, and `paths` is not filtered to exclude the `newer` entries. Concrete failure: a developer stages a view whose header says `fmt=2` (written by a newer ddflow) and whose body differs from what this ddflow renders, so `view_difference` returns `"newer"`. The message then prints `ddflow render` / `git add

` for that very path directly above the paragraph saying that path must not be regenerated by this ddflow. A user who follows the printed commands rewrites the file at the *older* format level with this build's renderer — the exact downgrade the new note (and D-compat-json-views) says must not happen — while the alternative instruction ("upgrade ddflow first") is only prose with no corresponding command. The `newer` paths should be excluded from `paths`/`_out_hint`/`git add` (or a separate message branch should be used when all wrong entries are `newer`), otherwise the emitted remedy contradicts the emitted warning.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce.py:1613-1636 (`_wrong_views` / `newer` handling)

chunk_findings.detail:
`view_difference` evaluates `head.fmt > FORMAT_LEVEL` *before* the body comparison, so a view whose body is byte-identical to a fresh render is still reported `"newer"` whenever its stamp carries a higher format level. That directly contradicts the function's own contract ("`""` when the body is the same (the first line, a stamp or none, is not compared)") and the D-compat-json-views rule that the freshness check "compares body and state, not bytes". Concretely, with `FORMAT_LEVEL == 1` and

    have = "<!-- ...truth. body-sha256=abcdef012345 fmt=2 -->\n# Board\n"
    want = "<!-- ...truth. body-sha256=abcdef012345 -->\n# Board\n"

`split_view(have)` yields `head.fmt == 2`, `body == want_body`, yet the function returns `"newer"` instead of `""`. The pre-commit hook / `rules_status` therefore fails (or claims an upgrade is required) for a view that needs no regeneration at all — the exact "every difference is from an older version" false classification this change is supposed to remove. The `head.fmt` check needs to be applied only after `body != want_body`.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new guard only refuses to write when the existing view's recorded format level is strictly greater than `FORMAT_LEVEL`; that is, the sole signal it consults is `fmt`. Per the stated design, `fmt` is a *format* level that is only carried above level 1 and only changes on format-breaking releases — ordinary content changes between ddflow releases keep the same `fmt`. So the comment "All checked before any is written: a view a newer ddflow wrote is not downgraded" does not hold for the common case.

Concrete failure: suppose ddflow v1.4 and v1.5 both run at `FORMAT_LEVEL == 2`. A user on v1.5 regenerates a view (say `rules.md`) whose body changed but whose header still says `fmt: 2`, and commits it. A user then runs the v1.4 installer over that repo. For that file `head.fmt (2) > FORMAT_LEVEL (2)` is `False`, so no `NewerView` is raised and the pre-check passes; the write loop then hits `p.read_text("utf-8") != new` and overwrites the v1.5 view with the older v1.4 body. That is exactly the downgrade the guard claims to prevent. The `Managed` state (`newer`/`older`/`edited`) that the decision introduces for this distinction is available via the `state` argument but is never consulted here, so a newer same-format view is indistinguishable from an edited one and is clobbered. Any file placed at a view path whose header cannot be parsed (`head is None`) likewise bypasses the guard entirely and is overwritten by the second loop.

chunk_findings.detail: The note now distinguishes four states but still appends a single remedy (`ddflow adopt --refresh-docs` rewrites them) for all of them, including `AD.DOC_NEWER`. Concretely: if a driver doc was written by a newer ddflow (state `DOC_NEWER`, labelled "newer format: upgrade ddflow") and the user is running an older ddflow that finds it, `_driver_drift_notes` emits `docs/... (newer format: upgrade ddflow) — ddflow adopt --refresh-docs rewrites them (and the rules blocks) and nothing else`. A user acting on the emitted instruction will run `--refresh-docs`, which rewrites the newer-format doc with this (older) ddflow's template, i.e. does exactly the downgrade the state label just warned against, silently discarding the newer content. The two halves of the same string contradict each other, and the remedy must be suppressed or replaced ("upgrade ddflow first") for `DOC_NEWER`. Before this change the note could not be emitted for a newer doc at all, so the contradiction is introduced here.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting/health.py:_driver_drift_notes

chunk_findings.detail:
A staged view whose header carries a format level above what this ddflow understands yields `why == "newer"`, so `wrong` contains `(p, "newer")` and, crucially, `paths = [p for p, _w in wrong]` includes `p`. The returned message then still prints the generic remediation:

    "    ddflow render" + _out_hint(paths),
    "    git add " + " ".join(shlex.quote(p) for p in paths),

so for input where the only differing view is a newer-format one (or a mix of `stale` + `newer`), the developer is told to regenerate and `git add` the very path the appended note says must not be touched ("A view written at a newer format level is not regenerated by this ddflow: upgrade ddflow first."). The two halves of the same message contradict each other, and a developer (or a hook/script that acts on the machine-readable `git add` line) will stage whatever this older ddflow renders for that path, i.e. downgrade the newer-format view — exactly the outcome D-compat-json-views is meant to prevent. Newer paths should be partitioned out of `paths`/`render`/`git add` and only drive the "upgrade ddflow first" branch; the count/listing must not present them as regenerable.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce.py `_wrong_views` (the `paths` / `ddflow render` / `git add` remediation block)

chunk_findings.detail: `view_difference` checks the newer-format level *before* it checks body equality, which contradicts its own contract ("`""` when the body is the same (the first line, a stamp or none, is not compared)") and produces a false "newer" for content that this version can reproduce byte-for-byte. Concretely: with `FORMAT_LEVEL == 1`, let `body = "X\n"` and call `view_difference(stamp_view(body, fmt=2), stamp_view(body, fmt=1))`. `stamp_view(body, fmt=2)` yields a first line containing `fmt=2`; `split_view` returns `fmt=2`; the first branch `head.fmt > FORMAT_LEVEL` is true, so the function returns `"newer"` and never reaches `body == want_body` — even though `have`'s body is identical to the fresh render's body. Callers such as `rules_status`/`driver_drift` then report the view as written by a newer ddflow and `write_views` refuses to regenerate it, when nothing actually needs regeneration. Since a bump of `FORMAT_LEVEL` re-stamps *every* view with the new level (via `stamp_view`'s default), a clone on the older level labels all of its unchanged views "newer". The body-equality check should take precedence (or the newer result should only be returned when a write would actually change the content).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/markdown.py:view_difference

chunk_findings.detail: The guard only null-checks the header object, not the `fmt` field, even though this change's own contract says generated views carry the format level "only above level 1" — i.e. a view written by the current version has **no** `fmt` line at all. Re-rendering any existing committed view (a level‑1 `rules.md`, for example) makes `split_view(...)[0]` return a header whose `fmt` is `None`; the expression then evaluates `None > FORMAT_LEVEL`, which raises `TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'int'` before anything is written, so every re-render of an existing view aborts with a traceback instead of regenerating the file. The check needs to treat an absent level as level 1, e.g. `head.fmt is not None and head.fmt > FORMAT_LEVEL` or `(head.fmt or FORMAT_LEVEL) > FORMAT_LEVEL`.

chunk_findings.detail: `_wrong_views` still builds `paths` from every entry of `wrong` and emits that same set both as the set to regenerate (`ddflow render` + `_out_hint(paths)`) and as the set to stage (`git add ...`), while simultaneously appending the note that a view written at a newer format level is *not* regenerated. The two statements are mutually exclusive for a `newer` path, and nothing in this change filters `newer` out of `paths`. Concretely, if a view on disk carries a higher `fmt` than `FORMAT_LEVEL`, enforce tells the user to render and `git add` a file that the view installer now refuses to write (the new `NewerView` path in `views.py`), i.e. it instructs a `ddflow render` that will fail and a stage of a file that was never regenerated. The new `NewerView` handling in `render` does not touch `_wrong_views`, so the finding still holds.

chunk_findings.detail: `view_difference` still evaluates `head.fmt > FORMAT_LEVEL` before the body comparison, so a view whose body is byte-identical to a fresh render is reported `"newer"` whenever its stamp carries a higher format level. That contradicts the function's own contract (`""` when the body is the same; the first line, stamp or none, is not compared) and the D-compat-json-views rule that freshness compares body and state, not bytes. With `FORMAT_LEVEL == 1` and a view body that matches the fresh render but a first line recording `fmt: 2`, the check returns `"newer"` instead of `""`, and callers then treat a correct view as stale. The intent text reiterates the body/state comparison; it does not change this ordering, so the finding is not answered.

chunk_findings.detail: The guard refuses to write only when the existing view's recorded `fmt` is strictly greater than `FORMAT_LEVEL`. Per the stated design, `fmt` is carried only above level 1 and changes only on format-breaking releases, so ordinary content changes between ddflow releases keep the same `fmt`. Therefore a view written by a newer ddflow release that did not bump `fmt` is silently overwritten/downgraded by an older ddflow with the same `FORMAT_LEVEL`, contradicting the comment "All checked before any is written: a view a newer ddflow wrote is not downgraded". Concrete input: ddflow release B writes a view with `fmt: 1` (content differs from release A); running release A (`FORMAT_LEVEL == 1`) on that repo passes the guard and rewrites the view, losing B's output. The change's reliance on `fmt` as the only signal (as stated in the intent) is precisely what makes this fail, so the finding still holds.

chunk_findings.detail:
`write_ddflow_gitignore` treats a file whose region markers are malformed the same as a file that has no region at all: the handler sets `body = None` and `have = None`, both splice guards fail, and control falls through to `replace_text(gi, GITIGNORE_REGION.render(DDFLOW_GITIGNORE))`, which overwrites the entire file. That contradicts the function's own contract ("A file with the region keeps everything outside it") and the design goal of `fsio.Managed` — surviving hand edits. Concrete input: `.ddflow/.gitignore` containing

    # >>> ddflow gitignore >>>
    <DDFLOW lines>
    # <<< ddflow gitignore <<<
    secrets/*.jsonl

where the user then deletes (or mangles) the `# <<< ...` line while adding `secrets/*.jsonl`. `body(have)` raises `RegionError`; `have`/`body` become `None`; the whole-file branch runs and the user's `secrets/*.jsonl` line is silently deleted rather than preserved or left untouched. The comment "broken markers: nothing to keep that can be told from damage" rationalizes discarding the file, but the content *outside* the region is exactly the user-owned text `Managed` exists to protect, so a malformed marker should leave the file alone (or splice conservatively) rather than replace it outright. Note this is distinct from the documented "no region at all" case, which is intentional; the bug is that the two cases are conflated into one destructive path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/adopt.py `write_ddflow_gitignore` (the `except RegionError:` branch)

chunk_findings.detail: This diff introduces `view_difference` returning a distinct `"newer"` value, but no code path here filters the `newer` entries out of the set of files the user is told to rewrite and stage. `_wrong_views` still builds `paths` from *every* entry in `wrong`, emits `" ddflow render"` + `_out_hint(paths)` and `" git add " + " ".join(...)`, and separately appends the note that a `newer` view "is not regenerated by this ddflow: upgrade ddflow first." Concretely, with `FORMAT_LEVEL == 1` and a committed view stamped `fmt=2` whose body differs from the current render, `view_difference` returns `"newer"`, that path is added to `wrong`, and the emitted instructions tell the user to `ddflow render` and `git add` exactly the file the adjacent note says cannot be regenerated. Part 4 does not touch enforce.py, so the fix (filtering `newer` out of `paths`) does not exist and the contradiction stands.

chunk_findings.detail: The guard in this change is corroborated by the new `NewerView(what, fmt)` and by `view_difference`, both of which key downgrade detection solely off `fmt` (`head.fmt > FORMAT_LEVEL`). But the stated design (D-compat-json-views) says `fmt` is a *format* level that is only carried above level 1 and only changes on format-breaking releases; ordinary content changes between ddflow releases keep the same `fmt`. Input: `FORMAT_LEVEL == 1`, and a view written by a newer ddflow that has the same `fmt=1` (so no fmt stamp) but a different body whose digest still matches its own stamp. `split_view` yields `fmt == 1`, `view_difference` yields `"stale"` (the digest matches, so not `"edited"`), and the guard therefore permits the write, silently downgrading the newer view's content — exactly what the comment "a view a newer ddflow wrote is not downgraded" claims cannot happen. Neither the body hash (which only certifies the file was not hand-edited) nor `fmt` can distinguish this case, so part 4 does not answer the finding.

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier finding still holds: `_wrong_views` collects `paths` from *every* entry in `wrong`, including the ones it classified `newer`, and then emits that same `paths` as the set to run `ddflow render` over and to `git add`, while simultaneously appending "A view written at a newer format level is not regenerated by this ddflow: upgrade ddflow first." Concrete input: a repository with one committed view whose head carries `fmt == 2` while the local `FORMAT_LEVEL == 1`. That single path is both the `newer` entry and the sole member of `paths`, so the tool tells the user to render and stage exactly the file it also says must not be regenerated; the two instructions are unsatisfiable for the same path, and following the render/add half silently downgrades the view. The part-5 hunk does not touch `enforce.py`, so nothing in this diff answers it.

The function evaluates `head.fmt > FORMAT_LEVEL` before the body comparison, so a view whose body (ignoring the first, stamp, line) is byte-identical to a fresh render is still reported `"newer"` whenever the stamp carries a higher format level. Input: `FORMAT_LEVEL == 1`, a committed view whose header line holds `fmt == 2` but whose remaining lines are identical to what this ddflow would emit. Expected `""` per the docstring's own contract ("`""` when the body is the same ... the first line ... is not compared") and per D-compat-json-views ("compares body and state, not bytes"); actual result `"newer"`. chunk_findings.detail: The new guard is exactly the code the previous finding criticized, and its reach is narrower than its comment claims. It raises only when `head.fmt > FORMAT_LEVEL`, and `fmt` is carried only above level 1 and changes only on format-breaking releases. Concrete input: a repository where a newer ddflow 1.y (same format level 1) wrote a view with different content — no `fmt`, and (at level 1) no stamp `> 1` for the guard to see. Now an older ddflow 1.x is run: for that path `head.fmt` is either absent (head `None`, check skipped) or defaults to `1`, so `1 > 1` is false, the guard does not fire, and the write loop below overwrites the newer content. The comment "a view a newer ddflow wrote is not downgraded" therefore only holds across format-bumping releases, not for ordinary content changes, which is the common case. The diff hunk *is* this guard, so it does not answer the finding.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/markdown.py:1142-1147 (the new pre-write guard)

chunk_findings.detail: The only probe added for the new "do not downgrade" guard stages a view with `fmt=2` (`MD.stamp_view(MD.GENERATED + "\nfrom the future\n", fmt=2)`), i.e. it only exercises the format-breaking case, which is exactly the case the guard's condition `existing.fmt > FORMAT_LEVEL` already covers. Per the stated design (D-compat-json-views), views carry no `ddflow=<version>` stamp and `fmt` is only carried above level 1 and only changes on format-breaking releases (the other test, `test_a_view_is_stamped_with_a_body_digest_and_no_version`, asserts `"ddflow=" not in first and "fmt=" not in first` for a level-1 view). So when a *newer ddflow release* writes a view while the format level is still 1 — the common case, since ordinary content changes keep the same `fmt` — and an older ddflow then runs `write_views`, the guard does not fire: `existing.fmt` (1) is not greater than `FORMAT_LEVEL` (1), the view's stamp hash matches its own body so it is not "edited", and the older render is written over it. Concretely: with `FORMAT_LEVEL == 1`, `docs/ddflow/QUEUE.md` containing a `fmt`-less (level-1) stamp with body `X` from a later release, running this ddflow renders body `Y` and overwrites the file; the comment "a view a newer ddflow wrote is not downgraded" does not hold, and the downgrade is silent. The added test passes without exercising this path, so it does not answer the earlier finding.

chunk_findings.detail: `_wrong_views` still builds `paths` from every entry of `wrong` and emits that same set both as the set to regenerate (`ddflow render` + `_out_hint(paths)`) and as the set to stage (`git add ...`), while simultaneously appending the note that a view written at a newer format level is *not* regenerated. The two statements are mutually exclusive for a `newer` path, and nothing in this change filters `newer` out of `paths`. Concretely, if a view on disk carries a higher `fmt` than `FORMAT_LEVEL`, enforce tells the user to render and `git add` a file that the view installer now refuses to write (the new `NewerView` path in `views.py`), i.e. it instructs a `ddflow render` that will fail and a stage of a file that was never regenerated. The new `NewerView` handling in `render` does not touch `_wrong_views`, so the finding still holds.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce.py:1613-1636 (`_wrong_views`)

chunk_findings.detail: `view_difference` still evaluates `head.fmt > FORMAT_LEVEL` before the body comparison, so a view whose body is byte-identical to a fresh render is reported `"newer"` whenever its stamp carries a higher format level. That contradicts the function's own contract (`""` when the body is the same; the first line, stamp or none, is not compared) and the D-compat-json-views rule that freshness compares body and state, not bytes. With `FORMAT_LEVEL == 1` and a view body that matches the fresh render but a first line recording `fmt: 2`, the check returns `"newer"` instead of `""`, and callers then treat a correct view as stale. The intent text reiterates the body/state comparison; it does not change this ordering, so the finding is not answered.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/markdown.py (`view_difference`)

chunk_findings.detail: The guard refuses to write only when the existing view's recorded `fmt` is strictly greater than `FORMAT_LEVEL`. Per the stated design, `fmt` is carried only above level 1 and changes only on format-breaking releases, so ordinary content changes between ddflow releases keep the same `fmt`. Therefore a view written by a newer ddflow release that did not bump `fmt` is silently overwritten/downgraded by an older ddflow with the same `FORMAT_LEVEL`, contradicting the comment "All checked before any is written: a view a newer ddflow wrote is not downgraded". Concrete input: ddflow release B writes a view with `fmt: 1` (content differs from release A); running release A (`FORMAT_LEVEL == 1`) on that repo passes the guard and rewrites the view, losing B's output. The change's reliance on `fmt` as the only signal (as stated in the intent) is precisely what makes this fail, so the finding still holds.

chunk_findings.detail:
`write_ddflow_gitignore` treats a file whose region markers are malformed the same as a file that has no region at all: the handler sets `body = None` and `have = None`, both splice guards fail, and control falls through to `replace_text(gi, GITIGNORE_REGION.render(DDFLOW_GITIGNORE))`, which overwrites the entire file. That contradicts the function's own contract ("A file with the region keeps everything outside it") and the design goal of `fsio.Managed` — surviving hand edits. Concrete input: `.ddflow/.gitignore` containing

    # >>> ddflow gitignore >>>
    <DDFLOW lines>
    # <<< ddflow gitignore <<<
    secrets/*.jsonl

where the user then deletes (or mangles) the `# <<< ...` line while adding `secrets/*.jsonl`. `body(have)` raises `RegionError`; `have`/`body` become `None`; the whole-file branch runs and the user's `secrets/*.jsonl` line is silently deleted rather than preserved or left untouched. The comment "broken markers: nothing to keep that can be told from damage" rationalizes discarding the file, but the content *outside* the region is exactly the user-owned text `Managed` exists to protect, so a malformed marker should leave the file alone (or splice conservatively) rather than replace it outright. Note this is distinct from the documented "no region at all" case, which is intentional; the bug is that the two cases are conflated into one destructive path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/adopt.py `write_ddflow_gitignore` (the `except RegionError:` branch)

chunk_findings.detail: This diff introduces `view_difference` returning a distinct `"newer"` value, but no code path here filters the `newer` entries out of the set of files the user is told to rewrite and stage. `_wrong_views` still builds `paths` from *every* entry in `wrong`, emits `" ddflow render"` + `_out_hint(paths)` and `" git add " + " ".join(...)`, and separately appends the note that a `newer` view "is not regenerated by this ddflow: upgrade ddflow first." Concretely, with `FORMAT_LEVEL == 1` and a committed view stamped `fmt=2` whose body differs from the current render, `view_difference` returns `"newer"`, that path is added to `wrong`, and the emitted instructions tell the user to `ddflow render` and `git add` exactly the file the adjacent note says cannot be regenerated. Part 4 does not touch enforce.py, so the fix (filtering `newer` out of `paths`) does not exist and the contradiction stands.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce.py:1613-1636 (`_wrong_views`)

chunk_findings.detail: The guard in this change is corroborated by the new `NewerView(what, fmt)` and by `view_difference`, both of which key downgrade detection solely off `fmt` (`head.fmt > FORMAT_LEVEL`). But the stated design (D-compat-json-views) says `fmt` is a *format* level that is only carried above level 1 and only changes on format-breaking releases; ordinary content changes between ddflow releases keep the same `fmt`. Input: `FORMAT_LEVEL == 1`, and a view written by a newer ddflow that has the same `fmt=1` (so no fmt stamp) but a different body whose digest still matches its own stamp. `split_view` yields `fmt == 1`, `view_difference` yields `"stale"` (the digest matches, so not `"edited"`), and the guard therefore permits the write, silently downgrading the newer view's content — exactly what the comment "a view a newer ddflow wrote is not downgraded" claims cannot happen. Neither the body hash (which only certifies the file was not hand-edited) nor `fmt` can distinguish this case, so part 4 does not answer the finding.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/markdown.py:1142-1147 (new pre-write guard)

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier finding still holds: `_wrong_views` collects `paths` from *every* entry in `wrong`, including the ones it classified `newer`, and then emits that same `paths` as the set to run `ddflow render` over and to `git add`, while simultaneously appending "A view written at a newer format level is not regenerated by this ddflow: upgrade ddflow first." Concrete input: a repository with one committed view whose head carries `fmt == 2` while the local `FORMAT_LEVEL == 1`. That single path is both the `newer` entry and the sole member of `paths`, so the tool tells the user to render and stage exactly the file it also says must not be regenerated; the two instructions are unsatisfiable for the same path, and following the render/add half silently downgrades the view. The part-5 hunk does not touch `enforce.py`, so nothing in this diff answers it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce.py:1613-1636 (`_wrong_views`)

chunk_findings.detail: This also still holds. The function evaluates `head.fmt > FORMAT_LEVEL` before the body comparison, so a view whose body (ignoring the first, stamp, line) is byte-identical to a fresh render is still reported `"newer"` whenever the stamp carries a higher format level. Input: `FORMAT_LEVEL == 1`, a committed view whose header line holds `fmt == 2` but whose remaining lines are identical to what this ddflow would emit. Expected `""` per the docstring's own contract ("`""` when the body is the same ... the first line ... is not compared") and per D-compat-json-views ("compares body and state, not bytes"); actual result `"newer"`. The part-5 hunk only edits the installer, not `view_difference`, so this is unaddressed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/markdown.py `view_difference`

chunk_findings.detail: The new guard is exactly the code the previous finding criticized, and its reach is narrower than its comment claims. It raises only when `head.fmt > FORMAT_LEVEL`, and `fmt` is carried only above level 1 and changes only on format-breaking releases. Concrete input: a repository where a newer ddflow 1.y (same format level 1) wrote a view with different content — no `fmt`, and (at level 1) no stamp `> 1` for the guard to see. Now an older ddflow 1.x is run: for that path `head.fmt` is either absent (head `None`, check skipped) or defaults to `1`, so `1 > 1` is false, the guard does not fire, and the write loop below overwrites the newer content. The comment "a view a newer ddflow wrote is not downgraded" therefore only holds across format-bumping releases, not for ordinary content changes, which is the common case. The diff hunk *is* this guard, so it does not answer the finding.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/markdown.py:1142-1147 (the new pre-write guard)

chunk_findings.detail: The only probe added for the new "do not downgrade" guard stages a view with `fmt=2` (`MD.stamp_view(MD.GENERATED + "\nfrom the future\n", fmt=2)`), i.e. it only exercises the format-breaking case, which is exactly the case the guard's condition `existing.fmt > FORMAT_LEVEL` already covers. Per the stated design (D-compat-json-views), views carry no `ddflow=<version>` stamp and `fmt` is only carried above level 1 and only changes on format-breaking releases (the other test, `test_a_view_is_stamped_with_a_body_digest_and_no_version`, asserts `"ddflow=" not in first and "fmt=" not in first` for a level-1 view). So when a *newer ddflow release* writes a view while the format level is still 1 — the common case, since ordinary content changes keep the same `fmt` — and an older ddflow then runs `write_views`, the guard does not fire: `existing.fmt` (1) is not greater than `FORMAT_LEVEL` (1), the view's stamp hash matches its own body so it is not "edited", and the older render is written over it. Concretely: with `FORMAT_LEVEL == 1`, `docs/ddflow/QUEUE.md` containing a `fmt`-less (level-1) stamp with body `X` from a later release, running this ddflow renders body `Y` and overwrites the file; the comment "a view a newer ddflow wrote is not downgraded" does not hold, and the downgrade is silent. The added test passes without exercising this path, so it does not answer the earlier finding.

chunk_findings.detail: The change's own contract is that generated views carry a format level "only above level 1", so a committed level‑1 view (e.g. `rules.md`) has no `fmt` line. `split_view(...)[0]` then yields a header whose `fmt` is `None`, and the guard only null-checks the header object, not the field: re-rendering any such view evaluates `None > FORMAT_LEVEL` and raises `TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'int'`. The intent states the no-`fmt` design but nothing in this part of the change adds the `head.fmt and ...` guard, so the crash remains.

chunk_findings.detail: The newer-format level is tested before body equality, contradicting the function's contract (`""` when the body is the same). Concretely, with `FORMAT_LEVEL == 1`, `view_difference(stamp_view("X\n", fmt=2), stamp_view("X\n", fmt=1))` yields a first line with `fmt=2`, so the level check fires and returns "newer" even though this version reproduces the body byte-for-byte. The intent ("the freshness check compares body and state, not bytes") does not necessarily reorder `view_difference` itself, and no hunk here changes it, so the false "newer" persists for the function and any caller that still uses it.

So for a staged view whose header carries a level above `FORMAT_LEVEL` (or a mix of `stale` + `newer`), the developer is instructed to run `ddflow render
