chunk_findings.detail: This is the code path the diff introduces and the guard is still unguarded against a missing `fmt`: `head = split_view(...)[0]` is null-checked, but `head.fmt` is not, and `if head is not None and head.fmt > FORMAT_LEVEL` evaluates `None > 1` for exactly the views this change says exist — the contract states generated views carry `fmt` "only above level 1", so a committed, level‑1 view produced by the current version parses to a header object whose `fmt` field is `None`. Concretely, in an existing project (e.g. `rules.md` committed by this same version) a re-render enters the first loop, `p.is_file()` is true, `head is not None` is true, and `head.fmt > FORMAT_LEVEL` raises `TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'int'` — the whole render aborts for every view (the loop deliberately checks all views before writing any). With `FORMAT_LEVEL == 1`, `body = "X\n"`, `view_difference(stamp_view(body, fmt=2), stamp_view(body, fmt=1))` returns `"newer"` even though the bodies are byte-identical and this version reproduces the content exactly. The developer is therefore told to regenerate exactly the view that the new `write_views` guard (`raise NewerView(...)`) refuses to write — the two behaviors contradict each other. chunk_findings.detail:
Still holds: the note distinguishes `DOC_NEWER` (labelled "newer format: upgrade ddflow") but appends the same single remedy for all states, `ddflow adopt --refresh-docs rewrites them (and the rules blocks) and nothing else`. For a doc written by a newer ddflow, that advice instructs rewriting (downgrading) the very file whose format this version cannot understand, which is precisely the operation the new `write_views` guard blocks. The untriaged status and the absence of any change to `_driver_drift_notes` mean the finding is unanswered.

chunk_findings.detail: The `_driver_drift_notes` path is the only part of the stated intent ("rules_status and driver_drift (services/adopt.py) stop calling every difference 'from an older version' using the Managed state (newer / older / edited)") that this change does not exercise or fix. The note distinguishes newer / older / edited, but still appends the same single remedy for every state: `ddflow adopt --refresh-docs rewrites them (and the rules blocks) and nothing else`. Concretely, when a driver doc was written by a newer ddflow (`DOC_NEWER`, labelled "newer format: upgrade ddflow") and the running ddflow is older, the emitted note tells the user to run `--refresh-docs`, which rewrites (downgrades) the newer-format doc. This diff adds tests for `enforce._wrong_views` and `RulesState.render`, but there is no probe for `_driver_drift_notes` and nothing in the diff shows the remedy has become state-dependent, so the earlier finding is not answered here.

chunk_findings.detail: `test_the_result_schemas_are_pinned` gates the golden rewrite on the *truthiness* of the environment variable instead of its documented value: `if os.environ.get("DDFLOW_UPDATE_GOLDEN"):`. Any non-empty string is truthy, so if the variable is exported as `DDFLOW_UPDATE_GOLDEN=0` (or `false`, `no`, `off`) — e.g. a shell profile or CI runner that defines the flag as `0` to mean "disabled" — the branch is taken: the test overwrites `tests/golden/json/result_schemas.json` with the freshly computed table, then asserts `GOLDEN.read_text(...) == table` against exactly what it just wrote. The assertion can never fail in that environment, so a field that was removed, renamed, or retyped (the very regression the test exists to catch) is silently accepted and the committed golden is mutated in place. The docstring only documents `DDFLOW_UPDATE_GOLDEN=1`, so `get(...) == "1"` is the intended gate.

chunk_findings.detail: The golden entry declares `"shape": "object"` and `"payload": "results"`, but its `output_schema.properties` contains only `schema` and `refusal`; `"results"` never appears. Every other object-shaped entry in the same file uses a JSON array for `payload` (e.g. ddflow_claim, ddflow_heartbeat, ddflow_complete) and repeats each listed name as a property in `output_schema.properties`. A consistency test that checks this invariant, or later code that trusts `payload` to build the schema, will either fail or emit a schema that silently omits the `results` field. The expected form is `"payload": ["results"]` with a matching `"results": {}` property, or the entry should be `"shape": "array"` with an `array_schema`.

chunk_findings.detail: The golden entry declares `"shape": "object"` and `"payload": "item"`, but its `output_schema.properties` contains only `schema` and `refusal`; `"item"` is absent. In all other object-shaped entries, the payload names appear verbatim in `output_schema.properties`. If a later slice applies this schema tag to a `show` result that actually contains an `item` field, the generated schema will not document that field, and a helper that assumes object-shaped payloads are lists will mishandle the string `"item"`.

chunk_findings.detail: The golden entry declares `"shape": "object"` and `"payload": "decision"`, but its `output_schema.properties` lacks any `"decision"` property. This breaks the file-wide invariant that object-shaped tools list each payload element as a property in `output_schema`. The likely defect is a copy-paste from an array-shaped entry: `decision_show` should either list `"payload": ["decision"]` with a matching `"decision": {}` property, or be modeled as `"shape": "array"` if it returns a bare array.

chunk_findings.detail: The asserted predicate contradicts the invariant the test documents. The comment above `_OWN_JSON` states "the list may only shrink" — i.e. `_OWN_JSON` is meant as an upper bound on the set of modules still printing their own JSON — but the assertion requires exact equality (`==`), not containment (`<=`). Given the environment described in the intent, `reporting.py` is held by another agent and will be migrated to `emit_json` independently of this change. The moment that lands, `reporting.py` stops containing a `json.dumps` call, so `own` becomes `[]`, while `_OWN_JSON` remains `{"reporting.py"}` because this test is not owned by that agent. `set(own)` is then `set()` and `set() == {"reporting.py"}` is False, so the test fails and turns CI red even though the property it exists to guard (no unapproved module writes its own JSON) still holds. The subset form `assert set(own) <= _OWN_JSON` would both catch a *new* module starting to print its own JSON and tolerate the allowlisted module being cleaned up.

chunk_findings.detail:
The scan set and the expected set disagree. The loop builds `own` only from
`root/"commands"/*.py`, `root/"context.py"`, and `root/"cli.py"`, where
`root = <repo>/ddflow/surfaces`. But `_OWN_JSON = {"reporting.py", "cli.py"}` names
`reporting.py`, which lives at `<repo>/ddflow/surfaces/reporting.py` — the module the
intent pairs with `cli.py` as "left / held by another agent". `reporting.py` is never
iterated (the author had to add `cli.py` and `context.py` explicitly precisely because
root-level modules are not covered by the `commands/*.py` glob, and `reporting.py` was
forgotten). Therefore `own` can never contain `"reporting.py"`: whether that file still
prints its own JSON or not, `own` is at most `{"cli.py"} ∪ {command modules with json}`,
while `_OWN_JSON` always contains `"reporting.py"`. Running the test on this tree yields
`set(own) == {'cli.py'}` versus `_OWN_JSON == {'cli.py', 'reporting.py'}`, i.e. the
assertion fails permanently (the only escape is a `ddflow/surfaces/commands/reporting.py`
existing, which would contradict the stated exemption). Fix by adding
`root / "reporting.py"` to the iterated list, or by dropping `"reporting.py"` from
`_OWN_JSON`.

chunk_findings.detail: The probe offered as a refutation only checks the current snapshot (`ls .../reporting.py` exists and the test passes today), which is a current-state check for a finding about a *future* state. chunk_findings.detail: `parsed_path` decides which subparser was entered by taking the first token in `argv` that happens to be a key of `sub.choices`, with no regard for option syntax. Any token that is *not* the command word but merely an option's argument is therefore misread as a subcommand, and the resulting tag is wrong. Concretely, for a parser where `gate` has subcommands `record` and `list` plus an option `--format` that takes a value, the invocation `ddflow gate --format record list` is parsed by argparse as `gate list --format record`, but `parsed_path` scans from `at` and stops at `record` (index 2 in `tokens`) because it is in `sub.choices`, returning `("gate", "record")`; `command_for_path` then falls through to `"_".join(path)` and tags the result `gate_record@n` instead of `gate_list@n`. The same scanner's guard `"--" in tokens[at:typed]` bails out as soon as a `--` precedes the matched word, but argparse still feeds positional arguments after `--` to the subparsers action, so `ddflow gate -- record` returns `("gate",)` and tags `gate@n` rather than `gate_record@n`. Both cases silently attach the wrong `schema` name to the object body.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py:parsed_path

chunk_findings.detail: `render.py` now imports `tag_body` from `.registry` at module top level. The module's own docstring previously guaranteed the opposite direction — "Standard library only: the surfaces **and the registry** may both import it" — i.e. the registry is an importer of this module, which was only safe because `render` was a leaf that depended on nothing but the stdlib. Adding a top-level `render -> registry` edge makes the graph bidirectional if the registry still does `from .render import dumps` (or similar). Concretely: `import ddflow.surfaces.registry` executes `registry.py`, which reaches its `from .render import ...`; that runs `render.py`, which reaches `from .registry import tag_body` while `ddflow.surfaces.registry` is present in `sys.modules` but only partially executed, so `tag_body` may not yet be bound and the import raises `ImportError: cannot import name 'tag_body' from partially initialized module`. This diff only changes `render.py`/tests, so unless a companion part removed the registry's import of `render`, either import order is now broken. (If the registry's import of `render` was in fact deleted elsewhere, this is moot; nothing in the shown diff does so.)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/render.py (`from .registry import tag_body`)

chunk_findings.detail: The helper pops the CLI `schema`, runs the bound on the untagged body, then re-inserts the **CLI** tag with `{"schema": tag, **from_cli}` and compares against `from_mcp`, which carries the **MCP** tag. That only passes when the two derivations coincide, but the stated intent derives the two names from different sources ("CLI name comes from the parsed command words ...; MCP name from the tool"), with explicit CLI tables for routed/flag-selected/verbless commands — i.e. the two tags are expected to differ for at least some commands. For any bounded tool whose CLI schema name differs from its tool name, `_surfaces_agree(tool, from_mcp, from_cli)` compares `{"schema": "<mcp>@n", ...}` against `{"schema": "<cli>@n", ...}` and fails. Additionally the re-insert puts `schema` first unconditionally, contradicting the "a refusal body keeps 'refusal' first" rule; if agreement is checked on rendered text rather than dict equality, a refusal body will mismatch (`{"schema":…, "refusal":…}` vs `{"refusal":…, "schema":…}`).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_api_layer.py (`tag = from_cli.pop("schema", None)` block, ~lines 580-586)

chunk_findings.detail: `command_for_path` decides which dependent tool serves a command by scanning the *raw* token list (`typed = set(argv)`) rather than the flags argparse actually recognized, so any token spelled like a flag flips the name even when argparse never treated it as one. `/--` is the clear case: `parsed_path` correctly stops at the terminator and returns `("import",)`, but `set(argv)` still contains the post-`--` token. Given `ddflow import -- --verify` (importing a file literally named `--verify`), the loop matches `(("import",), "--verify")` and returns `"import_verify"`, so the result body is tagged `import_verify@<n>` although the command executed is the one served by `ddflow_import`, and clients will select the wrong schema. The same holds for `ddflow companions -- --verify`. If you want to keep the token scan, it must stop at `--` (and, more generally, exclude tokens consumed as option values), otherwise the tested surface disagrees with what was parsed.

chunk_findings.detail: `_after_options` only consumes an option's value while the value does **not** start with `-`, but argparse does not use that rule. argparse's `_parse_optional` returns `None` (i.e. classifies the token as a positional/value, not an option) for the lone `"-"` and for tokens matching `^-\d+$` / `^-\d*\.\d+$` whenever the parser declares no option string with that shape (`_has_negative_number_optionals` is false by default). So the function diverges from the parser it is supposed to mirror exactly in the case the previous finding was about (an option sitting between a parent command and its subcommand word): with `argv = ["gate", "--count", "-1", "list"]` (a `gate` subparser having an option `--count` and the subcommands `record`/`list`), the loop skips `-1` because it starts with `-`, `_after_options` returns the index of `-1`, `"-1" not in sub.choices` is true, and `parsed_path` returns `("gate",)` instead of `("gate", "list")`. argparse itself parses this line successfully and enters `gate list`, so `command_for_path(("gate",), ...)` then emits the tag for the wrong command. The same happens for a stdin value: `ddflow gate --input - list` (`"--input"` consuming `"-"`), and note the inconsistency that the top of the same function already treats a lone `"-"` as a positional (`if not token.startswith("-") or token [REDACTED] "-": return at`), so `-` is accepted as a command boundary but not as an option value. Consuming a value only when it does not start with `-` therefore mis-resolves the subcommand and produces an incorrect top-level schema tag.

chunk_findings.detail: The new integration test claims to prove that *every* CLI command is named by a tool that serves it, but it calls `R.command_for_path(p, ROUTED_PATHS, COVERING_TOOLS)` with only three arguments. The flag-selected branch of `command_for_path` is only reachable when the invocation word list is supplied — as the companion test `test_a_flag_after_the_terminator_selects_nothing` demonstrates (`command_for_path(("import",), {}, {}, ["import", "--verify"]) == "import_verify"` versus `command_for_path(("import",), {}, {}, [...]) == "import"`). Without words, the test only ever computes the un-flagged name for a leaf path. Concretely, for the flag-selected command `ddflow import --verify`, whose tag is `import_verify`, the test evaluates the path `("import",)` and gets `"import"`; if no tool carries `import_verify` the assertion still passes (or the path is dropped entirely because `"import"` is in `EXEMPT_WORDS`/`EXEMPT_PATHS`). So a flag-selected CLI name that names no tool — exactly the category the intent says `command_for_path` was extended with "explicit tables for ... flag-selected" commands — goes undetected by the test whose stated job is to catch it.

chunk_findings.detail: The new slice only removes tokens *after* `--`; the flag is still matched by literal membership in the raw token list rather than by the option string argparse actually resolved. So the earlier finding (flag selection rebuilt from typed text instead of argparse's decision) still holds, just for a different input. Whenever argparse recognizes `--verify` from a different spelling, `command_for_path` misses it. Concretely, with `allow_abbrev` at its argparse default (nothing in this diff, or in `_WordsRecorder`'s use of the stock parser class, turns it off), `ddflow import --verif` is parsed as `--verify` and therefore *executes the verify variant*, but `typed` is `{"ddflow", "import", "--verif"}`, so the loop never matches `(("import",), "--verify")` and the function falls through to `routed`/`covering`/`"_".join(path)` and returns `"import"`. The result is tagged `import@<n>` for an operation whose MCP counterpart (`ddflow_import_verify`) is tagged `import_verify@<n>` — precisely the CLI/MCP divergence the change is supposed to eliminate. The same raw-token scan also misfires when `--verify` is swallowed as a value by an option declared with `nargs=argparse.REMAINDER` (argparse never treats it as a flag, but `typed` contains it). The author's probe (`test_a_flag_after_the_terminator_selects_nothing`) exercises only the `--` path, so it does not answer this residual case; the root cause is that the flag half of the decision was never moved onto argparse's parsed result the way `_WordsRecorder` did for the command words.

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion was updated to require the wire body to carry the new top-level `schema` tag (`set(body) == {"schema", "id"}`), but the failure message on the same line still says the body is wrong if it is not `{'id': ...}`. The message now contradicts the assertion it belongs to: the very body the assertion accepts (`{"schema": ..., "id": ...}`) is the one the message labels as failing. If this test ever fails, the diagnostic will report an expectation (`{'id': ...}` only) that the test no longer holds, sending debugging in the wrong direction (e.g., toward removal of the `schema` key rather than at the actual tagging path). The fix is to make the message state the expectation being checked; the message is part of the changed line, so it is stale as a direct result of this diff.

chunk_findings.detail: `full` is copied verbatim into `structuredContent`, but the very same object is put on the wire as text only after `json.dumps(full, separators=(",", ":"), default=str)` (line 307). The presence of `default=str` is an admission that `full` can contain values the `json` module cannot serialize natively (a `datetime`, `Decimal`, `set`, or any custom object) — otherwise the fallback would be dead code. `structuredContent` must itself be a JSON value, so this makes the two representations diverge exactly for those values. Concretely: a tool result containing a `datetime` (knob on, client revision >= 2025-06-18) produces `body = '{"at":"2024-01-01T00:00:00"}'` in the text block while `result["structuredContent"] = {"at": datetime(...)}` holds a live `datetime`. If the JSON-RPC writer serializes the response with a plain `json.dumps` (the same call that the text path deliberately avoided), the formerly-successful `tools/call` raises `TypeError: Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable`; if the writer re-applies `default=str`, the `structuredContent` a client validates against the tool's `outputSchema` no longer round-trips identically to the claimed "same object" text. Either way the object handed to `structuredContent` is not guaranteed to be JSON, which is what the field requires.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:311 (`_result`, `result["structuredContent"] = full`)

chunk_findings.detail: These three tools are reclassified from `"shape": "object"` to `"shape": "nested"` with `"output_schema": null` (previously they carried a real `{"type": "object", "properties": {"schema": {"const": "recall@1"}, "refusal": {}}, "additionalProperties": true}` / `decision_show@1` / `show@1` schema). Their results are still JSON objects — that is why they previously had a `type: object` output schema and why their results carry the `schema` tag plus a single payload field (`results` / `decision` / `item`); the reclassification only changes how the registry labels the shape, it does not change the wire result. But the new `mcp.output_schemas` help text added in this same diff (tests/golden/__snapshots__/test_golden_outputs.ambr, the `mcp.output_schemas = 'off'` block) promises: "Whether `tools/list` declares an `outputSchema` for every tool whose result is a JSON object, and a call returns that object also as `structuredContent`" and "each object tool lists `{"type": "object", "properties": {...}}`". With the knob `on`, a client will therefore get an `outputSchema` for the other object tools but **none** for `ddflow_recall`, `ddflow_decision_show`, and `ddflow_show`, even though their results are JSON objects — silently, since `"nested"` has neither `output_schema` nor `array_schema` populated (both are `null`), so the `_meta["ddflow/outputSchema"]` fallback reserved for bare-array tools does not apply either. Either the help text overstates the guarantee ("every tool whose result is a JSON object") or these three tools are incorrectly excluded from the very feature they were object results for; the diff cannot satisfy both.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/json/result_schemas.json (ddflow_recall / ddflow_decision_show / ddflow_show)

chunk_findings.detail:
The text block and `structuredContent` are built from the same `full` dict but go through different normalization. The text path deliberately does `json.dumps(full, separators=(",", ":"), default=str)`, i.e. the author of this code expects `full` to be able to contain values that are not JSON-native (paths, `Decimal`, `datetime`, or similar) and coerces them to strings. The new line hands the *raw* `full` to the MCP result:

```python
    if structured and isinstance(full, dict) and out.exit != 1:
        result["structuredContent"] = full
```

So for the exact inputs the `default=str` fallback exists for, the two representations of "the same object" diverge: either the JSON-RPC writer that serializes the whole result does not apply `default=str` (as is typical), in which case `json.dumps` on the response raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` and a modern client with the knob on gets a broken/errored response for a call that succeeds for an older client — `typ`/`exit` metadata is already rendered by the time the exception happens, so the failure is total, not a degraded field; or the writer *does* apply `default=str`, in which case the stringified value is what a client validates against the `outputSchema` that `_result_declaration` just published, and any field the registry schema describes as a non-string (object/number) now arrives as a string, failing client-side validation. Either way, turning `[mcp].output_schemas` on changes the correctness of the result for a class of tool payloads that the off path renders fine, and the fix is to declare `structuredContent` from the same normalized structure that produced `body` (e.g. `json.loads(body)`), not from `full`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:309-312 (`_tool_result`, the new `structuredContent` assignment)

chunk_findings.detail: The change flips these three tools from `"shape": "object"` (with a non-null `output_schema`) to `"shape": "nested"` with `"output_schema": null` (and `array_schema` already null). The stated intent is that when `mcp.output_schemas=on` and the client's revision is >= 2025-06-18, `tools/list` declares an `outputSchema` for **each object-result tool** (from `registry.output_schema`) and `tools/call` returns that object also as `structuredContent`. These three tools still have JSON-object results — `ddflow_show` returns an `item` record, `ddflow_decision_show` returns a `decision` record, `ddflow_recall` returns a `results` record, and all three were classified as `object` before this change. Since their `registry.output_schema` is now `null`, a modern client with `output_schemas=on` calling, e.g., `ddflow_show` gets no `outputSchema` in `tools/list` and no `structuredContent` in the `tools/call` result: the feature silently does nothing for them, contradicting the documented promise ("each object tool lists …" and "`tools/call` returns the object also as `structuredContent`"). Either the nested results are still objects and must keep/get a schema (the golden data is wrong), or the documented behaviour must exclude `nested` tools; as written the two disagree.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/json/result_schemas.json (ddflow_recall, ddflow_show, ddflow_decision_show)

chunk_findings.detail:
For the pre-2025-06-18 revisions (`2024-11-05`, `2025-03-26`) this test only asserts that no tool dict contains an `outputSchema` key:

```python
assert not any("outputSchema" in t for t in _tools(server).values())
```

The intent gates the whole declaration on the revision — both the per-object `outputSchema` *and* the bare-array tool's schema under `_meta['ddflow/outputSchema']`. The sibling test `test_off_by_default_nothing_is_declared` checks both (`"outputSchema" in t or "_meta" in t`), so the omission here is asymmetric. Concretely: if the version gate were applied only to the object `outputSchema` and the `_meta` array schema were emitted unconditionally (i.e. also for a client that negotiated `2024-11-05`), `tools/list` would return, e.g., `{"name": "ddflow_progress", ..., "_meta": {"ddflow/outputSchema": {...}}}` and this test would still pass, even though the function's name claims the client is "served as before". The check should also assert that no tool carries `_meta` (at minimum no `ddflow/outputSchema` key) for these revisions.

chunk_findings.detail: `_result_declaration` returns `{}` for `show`, `decision_show` and `recall` because the registry now classifies them as `"shape": "nested"` with `"output_schema": null`, so `_REGISTRY.output_schema(...)` yields None and `array_schema(...)` yields None. Their results are still plain JSON objects with declared fields (`schema: show@1` plus a payload field, etc.), which is why they previously advertised a real `{"type":"object", ...}` `outputSchema`. The earlier triage's probe is documentation ("README and knob doc now say nested tools declare none"), but a doc sentence does not change the emitted `tools/list` entries, so a client that validates or deserializes these three tools' results via `outputSchema` (and now via `structuredContent`, which `_result` will still emit for them since their `full` is a dict) gets no declaration to validate against, while every other object-result tool is declared. Documentation of the gap is not a fix for the gap.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:_result_declaration (and tests/golden/json/result_schemas.json)

chunk_findings.detail: The reclassification is not answered by the author's triage. The code change makes `result_shape` return `"nested"` for *every* tool whose `payload` is a non-empty string that is not in `ARRAY_PAYLOADS`, so `ddflow_show`, `ddflow_decision_show` and `ddflow_recall` now fall into the "declare no outputSchema" bucket. Their results are unchanged and are still JSON objects with declared fields (the `schema` tag plus the payload field), which is exactly the contract the knob advertises ("declare an outputSchema for each object-result tool with declared fields"). Concretely: with a repo whose config sets `[mcp].output_schemas = on`, a client at revision >= 2025-06-18 calls `tools/list`; the declaration for `ddflow_show` / `ddflow_decision_show` / `ddflow_recall` contains no `outputSchema` (and consequently `tools/call` for them sets no `structuredContent`), even though the knob promises a schema for object-result tools with declared fields. The only "fix" recorded for this finding is a README/knob-doc sentence carving these three names out; text in a doc does not change the code path or the emitted declaration, so the finding still holds. Either the declaration logic should key "nested" off something narrower than "any string payload" (so genuine object/record results still declare a schema), or the knob's stated contract needs to actually match the code.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py `result_shape` (and tests/golden/json/result_schemas.json)

chunk_findings.detail: The reclassification triage for the previous finding 2 claims the fix is that "README and knob doc now say 'tool whose result is a JSON object of declared fields (not show, decision_show, recall...)'". The knob doc added in this very diff does not say that. It states the option controls whether `tools/list` "declares an `outputSchema` for every tool whose result is a JSON object" and that "each object tool" lists one; there is no qualifier and no exclusion anywhere in the added block. Meanwhile the same diff (tests/golden/json/result_schemas.json) sets `output_schema: null` for `ddflow_show`, `ddflow_decision_show` and `ddflow_recall`, whose results are still JSON objects (they even carry `"schema": "show@1"` / `decision_show@1` / `recall@1` plus a payload field). So the user-facing config help contradicts the behaviour it is documenting: a reader is told these tools get an `outputSchema` when they do not. The probe cited in the triage therefore does not answer the finding as far as the knob doc is concerned; the doc needs to name the nested-record exclusion (or the sentence must be qualified) before finding 2 can be considered resolved. This is documentation only (no runtime effect), hence LOW.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/__snapshots__/test_golden_outputs.ambr (the `mcp.output_schemas` knob doc)

chunk_findings.detail: The knob description that is added by this diff still reads: "Whether `tools/list` declares an `outputSchema` for every tool whose result is a JSON object ... `on`: each object tool lists `{"type": "object", "properties": {"schema": {"const": "<tool>@<n>"}, <its declared fields>: {}}}` ... and a bare-array tool lists its schema under `_meta["ddflow/outputSchema"]`". Nested tools are never mentioned and no exclusion is stated. But in the same diff `tests/golden/json/result_schemas.json` flips `ddflow_show`, `ddflow_decision_show` and `ddflow_recall` from `"shape": "object"` to `"shape": "nested"` with `"output_schema": null`. Those three tools return JSON objects (their old `output_schema` was `{"type":"object",...}` and their top-level result is still an object with `payload` `item`/`decision`/`results`), so the help text promises an `outputSchema` for them while they will in fact declare none. The triage for finding #2 claims "README and knob doc now say 'tool whose result is a JSON object of declared fields (not show, decision_show, recall...)'", but the knob doc rendered here has neither "of declared fields" nor the "(not show, decision_show, recall...)" carve-out, so the stated fix is not present in this help text and the finding still holds. (The same sentence also unconditionally promises `structuredContent`, without the "not on isError" caveat, so an error result's `isError: true` response is over-described as well.)

chunk_findings.detail: The old loop only kept entries with a positive score (`if score > 0: scored.append(...)`), so `_rank` returned *only* entries sharing at least one query token. The new code forwards the raw `scores` mapping from `bm25(...)` straight into `sorted(scores, ...)`. A general-purpose BM25 ranker returns a score for every document it is given (unmatched docs get exactly `0.0`), so the zero-score entries are no longer dropped — they are merely sorted to the end and can still be admitted by `order[:limit]`. Concrete input: `entries` has 4 skills, only one of which contains the query token, and `limit=3`. Before, `scored` contained a single element and `_rank` returned `[matching_entry]`. Now `order` contains all four indices, and `order[:3]` yields the matching skill plus two non-matching skills (tie-broken by `path`). The output set/order differs from the previous behaviour whenever the number of token-sharing entries is less than `limit`. (If `searchcore/rank.bm25` internally filters `score > 0` the two are equivalent, but nothing in this hunk restores that filter, so the refactor silently relies on an unshown contract to preserve behaviour.)

chunk_findings.detail: The rewrite drops the `if score > 0:` guard that the old loop used to build `scored`. The old body appended an entry only when it had a positive BM25 score (i.e. it contained at least one query token), so `relevant()` could return fewer than `limit` results — or `[]` — when few/no entries matched. The new body feeds the whole `scores` mapping straight into the sort and then slices `order[:limit]`, so it returns `limit` entries whenever `bm25` emits an entry for every document (score 0 included). Concretely: with `MAX_FILES`-worth of entries, a query whose tokens appear in exactly one entry, and `limit=3`, the old code returns that single entry, while the new code returns it plus two zero-scoring entries (the lexicographically-first paths). For a query whose tokens match no entry at all, the old code returns `[]`, whereas the new code returns the first `limit` entries sorted by `path` — the caller now gets named "relevant" skills that share no term with the query. Same failure exists for the `lessons`/`search` callers if `bm25` does not itself discard zero scores.

chunk_findings.detail:
The old code ran the record enumerators *unconditionally*:

```python
out = _item_docs(st, cfg, kinds) + _record_docs(st, cfg, kinds)   # always executed
if kinds & {"session", "prompt"}: ...
if "log" in kinds: ...
```

The new code expresses the same rows as a `FuncSource` whose `kinds` are `tuple(sorted(_RECORD_SOURCES))`. If the registry (as `FuncSource.kinds` implies) only invokes a source when its `kinds` intersect the requested `kinds`, this call is now *conditional*, which it never was. Concretely, a request that reaches `_docs` with an empty kind set — the exact case the old code answered with "item + record docs and no session/log docs", because `_item_docs`/`_record_docs` are called unconditionally while sessions/log are gated off by `kinds & {...}` / `"log" in kinds` — now hits an empty intersection with `_RECORD_SOURCES`. Under the natural gate `if not (set(src.kinds) & kinds): continue`, `gather(Ctx(st, events, cfg), set())` skips *every* source and returns `[]`, whereas the old function returned `_item_docs(st, cfg, set()) + _record_docs(st, cfg, set())` (non-empty when empty kinds means "no type filter", the only reading under which the old unconditional call makes sense). Under the alternative "empty kinds runs everything" gate, the result instead gains the session/log rows the old code deliberately excluded for `kinds == set()`. Either way the rows are not identical, which is precisely the promise ("output must stay identical") the change is supposed to keep. The same asymmetry bites for any `kinds` set that is disjoint from `_RECORD_SOURCES`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py:139 (`register(FuncSource("records", tuple(sorted(_RECORD_SOURCES)), ...))`)

chunk_findings.detail: The stated invariant of the change is "search() … output must stay identical", yet the only added test never calls `_docs`/`gather`, never compares a row list against the old enumerator triple, and asserts nothing about row identity, order of emitted rows, or duplicates. It only inspects registry metadata (names, `src.kinds`, `S.SOURCES`). A refactor that dropped the `records` source, reordered `records`/`sessions`/`log` inside `gather`, double-registered a source, or returned a generator instead of a list would pass this test unchanged. So the invariant the diff claims to preserve is entirely untested; the finding above is exactly one of the regressions this test cannot catch.

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor deletes `re.search(query, combined, re.IGNORECASE)` and replaces it with a pattern obtained from `check_regex(query)`, which is invoked with **no flags**. The neighbouring substring tests use `query_lower in combined`, i.e. `combined` is the lower-cased text of the rule, so the removed `re.IGNORECASE` was exactly what allowed an upper/mixed-case pattern to hit lower-cased rule text. Concretely: with a rule whose combined text is `"todo: refactor the parser"`, the command `ddflow rule search --regex "TODO"` used to match (`re.search("TODO", "todo: ...", re.IGNORECASE)` → match, score 0.8, rule listed). With the new code the pattern is whatever `check_regex` compiles; unless `check_regex` hard-codes `re.IGNORECASE`, `rx.search(combined)` returns `None` and the rule is silently dropped — a result change beyond the stated "unguarded regex / compile error" fix. The call site should either pass the flags through or the shared helper must be confirmed to compile case-insensitively.

chunk_findings.detail: The new fallback drops the row filter entirely: it does `select * from {table}` with no predicate, computes `bm25(docs, qtoks)` over *every* row, and then returns `rows[i] for i in order[:limit]`. The shared ranker is a pure scorer over the candidates `gather` already matched in the search core (see `from .searchcore.hit import FuncSource, gather, register`), so it assigns `0.0` to documents that contain none of `qtoks` rather than dropping them. Consequently a query that matches nothing no longer returns `[]`: `_like_terms(query)` is non-empty (so the guard passes), `qtoks` may be non-empty, every score is `0.0`, `sorted(scores, key=lambda i: (-scores[i], str(rows[i].get("id",""))))` yields all indices ordered by id, and `order[:limit]` returns the `limit` lexicographically-smallest-id rows. Concrete input: on a build without FTS5, search for a term that occurs in no rule (e.g. `zzzznope`). Old code ran `... where ... like '%zzzznope%'`, matched no row, and returned `[]`; the new code returns `limit` unrelated rules. That is a result-set change beyond the stated intent of switching from substring-LIKE to BM25 *ranking*, and it is user-visible (a no-match search now reports bogus matches). A score threshold / membership check (e.g. keep only `i` where `scores[i] > 0`, or intersect with the token-matched set) is required, and the same happens when the guard passes but `textsim.tokens(query)` is empty (all-stopword query), since `bm25(docs, [])` also scores every row `0.0`.

chunk_findings.detail: The old code matched regexes case-insensitively: `re.search(query, combined, re.IGNORECASE)`. The new code compiles the pattern once via `check_regex` and then calls `rx.search(combined)` with no flags at the call site, so the match becomes whatever flags `check_regex` compiled with. The safety check is about ReDoS/compile validity, not matching semantics, so a plain `re.compile(pattern)` loses the `IGNORECASE` that the rules search previously had. This matters concretely because the rule text is normalized for the exact branch (`query_lower in combined`), i.e. `combined` is lowercased; compare by indexing with `("rules", query, regex, exact)` and construct `combined` analogously to the existing code, and observe the difference. Call `rules_search(repo, "Foo", regex=True)` with a rule whose body contains `... foo ...`: previously `re.search("Foo", combined, re.IGNORECASE)` matched and assigned `score = 0.8`, so the rule was returned as a ranked hit; now `rx.search(combined)` compiles `Foo` case-sensitively, finds no match in the lowercase `combined`, leaves `score` unset, and the rule is dropped from the result (a case change in the pattern is silently treated as "no matching rules" — exit 2 — instead of a hit). This is outside the stated intent (refusing unsafe patterns and BM25 ranking), which says nothing about making the regex branch case-sensitive.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new fallback no longer filters on relevance: it scores *every* row in the table with `bm25(docs, qtoks)`, sorts all of them, and then slices `[:limit]` unconditionally. A standard BM25 ranker returns one score per document (0 for documents containing none of the query terms), so any query that matches fewer than `limit` rows — including a query that matches nothing at all — returns unrelated rules.

Concrete case: table has 20 lessons, none containing the term `zzzz`. The old code did `select * from {table} where ... like '%zzzz%' limit ?` and returned `[]`. The new code: `_like_terms("zzzz")` is non-empty, so the guard passes; `qtoks = ["zzzz"]`; every document's score is 0; `sorted` orders all indices by the id tie-break; `order[:limit]` yields `limit` rows and the fallback returns rules that do not contain `zzzz`. The case is worse when there is exactly one match and `limit` is large (e.g. the default 20): one relevant rule is padded with 19 irrelevant ones.

This also re-opens the cross-build divergence the change claims to remove: the FTS5 branch above returns only rows that actually matched (`out` is built from the FTS result set), while this fallback now returns `limit` rows regardless of match, so the same query returns a different result *count* on a machine whose SQLite lacks FTS5. The correct tail would filter zero scores (or rank only documents that share at least one term with `qtoks`) before slicing.

chunk_findings.detail: The loop drives `rule search --regex ` with the pattern `(a)\1` and demands exit code 3. The stated intent for this change is that `--regex` now goes through `check_regex` so that *unguarded/catastrophic* patterns are refused and *compile errors* stop reading as "No rules found". A back-reference is neither of those: `re.compile(r"(a)\1")` succeeds in Python, and matching `(a)\1` is not catastrophic (the referenced group captures a single literal char), so it is a perfectly usable search pattern. Consequently `rule search --regex '(a)\1'` now exits 3 with no results where it previously returned the rules whose title/content contain `aa` — a user-visible refusal of a valid pattern that the intent does not cover. The only way this assertion can pass is if `check_regex` rejects back-references outright (in which case the change silently refuses valid patterns, as above); if `check_regex` does not reject back-references, then the pattern compiles, search returns nothing, the CLI exits 0, and this assertion fails. Either branch is a defect the intent does not sanction: a benign, compilable pattern is being forced into the "refused" class alongside `(a+)+b` and `(`.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten fallback has no predicate at all: it selects every row of the table, scores them, and returns `order[:limit]`. The shared ranker is only a scorer, so a document containing none of `qtoks` contributes nothing and gets score `0.0` — it is not dropped. Concretely, on a table whose rows do not contain `zzzqqq`: `_like_terms("zzzqqq")` yields `["zzzqqq"]`, so `qtoks` is non-empty and the `if not qtoks: return []` guard is not taken; `select * from {table}` returns all rows; every `bm25` score is `0.0`; `sorted(...)` still yields all indices, so `[rows[i] for i in order[:limit]]` returns `limit` rows that share no term with the query. The old code (`where c like '%t%'`) returned `[]` for that query, so this is a behavior regression for any non-matching query. This is the previously-reported finding #2, and the refutation does not answer it: the cited probes (`tests/test_search_core.py::test_the_like_fallback_returns_only_rows_that_share_a_term` / `::test_the_like_fallback_ranks_best_first`) exercise the search-core pipeline, where `gather` has already restricted the candidate set to documents that matched, so "returns only rows that share a term" holds there without `bm25` ever having to filter. The store path changed here calls `bm25(docs, qtoks)` directly over *every* row with no `gather` in front of it, which is exactly the case the probe does not cover.

chunk_findings.detail: The new fallback drops the `limit ?` clause that the old code passed to SQLite and instead reads and tokenizes the *entire* table on every call: `rows = [dict(r) for r in con.execute(f"select * from {table}")]`, then `docs = [_fallback_words(...) for r in rows]` and `bm25(docs, qtoks)`. The old query was `select * from {table} where ... limit ?`, so work was bounded by a single `LIMIT`. On the FTS5-less environment this code path exists for – exactly the environment the comment says it targets – a lesson/rule table that grows to, say, 100k rows with a few KB of text per row causes every `search` invocation to allocate the full table (all columns) and run `textsim.words`/`textsim.stem` over every text column of every row, i.e. O(total corpus) CPU and memory per query regardless of how few rows match, with the result set sliced to `limit` only at the very end (`order[:limit]`). A query with a single rare term that matches one row still tokenizes the whole table; the previous implementation returned after the SQL engine had examined at most `limit` rows. Filtering candidates in SQL (or at least limiting the loaded column set/rows) is needed to keep the fallback from turning into an unbounded scan that can OOM or stall on large stores.

data.body:
Planned work has 6 separate budgeted injectors (B-rw-inject, B-skills-context, B-rules-context-gate/B-rules-rag, B-dt-rules guidance, B-ds-rag, B202 digest) and 2 embedding backends (B-semantic-recall infra/embed.py, B-ds-semantic). Land the pack (ranked candidates from search-core -> dedupe by textsim -> cut by textcut under a token budget -> cite -> fence via core/provenance) and the Embedder contract (stdin JSON texts -> vectors, model id, timeout, [rag] extra or companion, unavailable when absent) before them; the existing brief/recall budgets migrate first with goldens. One shared budget vocabulary replaces ~6 per-feature token knobs (aliases kept).

D-unify (operator 2026-10-06): Extra [rag] = model2vec + sqlite-vec (one adapter module); never downloads a model at runtime (operator points to a local model dir); unavailable without it, BM25 fallback.

Unification survey 2026-10-06: Fix the globs: api/knowledge.py and api/lifecycle.py are packages now. Also: one approx_tokens(text) and chars_for(tokens) (markdown.py:425, markdown.py:1081/1085-1086, brief.py:189 without max(1, ...)). The recall budget is enforced twice with different meanings (mcp_bound.py:212-244 counts JSON size and takes one hit per kind in turn; commands/knowledge.py:204-221 counts rendered characters in table order and stops at the first overflow), while the API (retrieval.py:59) takes max_chars and enforces nothing; the default 4000 is defined three times. Enforce in the API layer with one Budget(tokens|chars), and state the unit of each budget knob (brief tokens; recall, memory, snippet and compaction characters).

Split into: B-uni-context-pack.1-budget, B-uni-context-pack.2-pack, B-uni-context-pack.3-embedder.
